Costco is general merchandise retail where customers need no help beyond the checkout lane; Home Depot is specialty retail, where price, selection, and convenience — the "trinity" — aren't enough. You also need something unique to the category — like a tire shop that mounts tires, a beauty store that lets you try makeup, or Apple with its Genius Bar. Home Depot essentially invented "customer service" in the home improvement category itself.

1:35:12 Low gross margin relies on turnover, not margin percentage
Home Depot's warehouse model has two structural disadvantages: an extremely high SKU count and a very large in-store service staff, making rapid turnover operationally difficult, and per-store labor costs higher than the club model. Ben says what holds it all together is "manufacturing buying frenzy" — with so many SKUs, you must give people a reason to buy them all. The key line: what feeds the company is not the gross margin percentage but gross profit dollars. So it needs enough volume and fast enough turnover that the gross profit dollars add up to justify the inventory the store carries. Once volume is built, it can place bigger orders with suppliers, demand lower prices, pass the savings to customers, and spin the wheel faster.

1:53:38 It invented the national chain, so no one else could buy nationally
Home Depot's early philosophy was radical decentralization, letting stores use local knowledge to decide what and how much to stock; Bernie estimated this made individual store sales 15% to 20% higher. But as scale grew, the costs of decentralization outweighed the benefits: operational chaos, inability to unify systems and technology, and countless decision-makers and negotiators facing the same suppliers, unable to get the best prices. Ben points out a key fact: this problem didn't exist for others because the very concept of a "national hardware chain" was invented by Home Depot — before it, no one bought nationally, so there was no national purchasing opportunity.

2:12:04 Replacing knowledgeable staff with 16-year-old cashiers
Nardelli replaced a large portion of store associates with part-time general retail labor, effectively killing the philosophy of "a knowledgeable person sells you a 25-cent washer, fixes your sink, and brings in the big follow-on order." According to Arvind's research, from 2000 to 2006 store associates dropped from 200 to 170, a 15% reduction. Store manager standards also changed, favoring college-educated candidates — while the associates hired had no college degrees, essentially telling them they were locked into jobs with no promotion path. The result: customer satisfaction fell to the lowest among major U.S. retailers, while revenue and profit doubled.

2:20:10 If pay isn't tied to the stock, you won't store value in the company
Ben nails the incentive misalignment: if compensation is tied to the stock price, you don't care about current earnings; you want investors to believe you're storing long-term value in the company, so you keep prices low, drive volume, and make customers ecstatic. If compensation is tied to today's numbers, you don't store value in the company; you just pump today's numbers. David calls this "the paradoxical misalignment of incentives." Nardelli refused to tie any compensation to the stock price, arguing it was the only metric he couldn't control — which directly contradicted the core of the company model: the associate's promise had always been "I do well, the stock goes up, I get rich."

item.title: A Soviet Spy's Secret Shame Nearly Stopped World War III
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-historyhit-一个苏联间谍的难言之隐-差点阻止了第三次世界大战/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-historyhit-一个苏联间谍的难言之隐-差点阻止了第三次世界大战/
item.description: In 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran walked in to MI6 — not for money or ideology, but because he believed the West could cure his erectile dysfunction. The intelligence he handed over led the US and Britain to give the Soviets' coup plan to the Iranians.
item.content:encoded:
In 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran walked in to MI6 — not for money or ideology, but because he believed the West could cure his erectile dysfunction. The intelligence he handed over led the US and Britain to give the Soviets' coup plan to the Iranians.

Ben Macintyre tells a Cold War spy story that has never been told, with astonishing detail and tight pacing — though the information density is concentrated in the second half, on the coup and its aftermath, while the setup runs long.

0:00 A spy story that has never been told
Ben Macintyre's new book Redwood tells a Cold War story that had never been made public before: in 1981, a senior KGB officer in Tehran, Vladimir Kuzichkin, walked in to MI6 and became a double agent codenamed ‘Redwood’. The intelligence he provided revealed that the Soviets were plotting a coup through the Iranian communist Tudeh Party to overthrow Khomeini's government, after which the Red Army would cross into Iran from Afghanistan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan. The Pentagon's answer to that was nuclear strikes — because conventional forces were not enough to stop a full Soviet invasion. What makes the story so strange is that Kuzichkin's motive for defecting was intensely personal: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed Western medicine could cure him.

3:01 1981 came closer to nuclear war than the Cuban Missile Crisis
Macintyre points out that 1981 was one of the closest moments of nuclear confrontation in the Cold War, second only to the Cuban Missile Crisis. After the Iranian Revolution, every faction — nationalists, liberals, communists and Islamists — was fighting for power, and Tehran became a ‘seething cauldron of spies’. The CIA, MI6 and the KGB all poured in at once. The Soviets had just invaded Afghanistan and were doing well, while the Americans were desperate to re-establish a foothold in the Middle East. If the Soviets took Iran, they could control warm-water ports and oil fields and win the Cold War. So the Pentagon was already drawing up nuclear options, including using portable nuclear weapons to blow up mountain ranges and block Soviet armour.

8:18 The CIA was blind in Tehran; MI6 stayed on in breach of the rules
After the Iran hostage crisis, the CIA was thrown out of Tehran and had no human intelligence in Iran at all, leaving it ignorant of a possible Soviet coup. The only service still capable of operating was MI6, but the condition on which Britain kept a diplomatic mission in 1981 was ‘no spying of any kind’. MI6 sent Ian McCready in anyway, under commercial counsellor cover — a huge gamble by the British government. McCready's instructions were ‘do nothing, recruit no one, keep your head down’ — because if he was caught, the Iranians would take the entire embassy hostage. He could only communicate with London using a Second World War cipher machine called RockX, an extremely cumbersome device of which only two existed in the world.

12:29 The motive for defecting was impotence, not money or ideology
Kuzichkin was a senior officer at the KGB residency in Tehran, responsible for the whole Middle East illegals programme, and the only defector who understood how the illegals system worked. He walked in to MI6 and offered to spy for the West. The spy world has an acronym, MICE — money, ideology, coercion, ego — but Kuzichkin fitted none of the categories. Part of it was alienation from the regime, but the root cause was this: he suffered from erectile dysfunction and believed the West had a drug that could cure it. He had just married, he loved his wife, and he could not reveal the secret to his KGB colleagues or to Soviet doctors. McCready did not mock him or exploit him; he treated it with extreme seriousness, and even sent MI6 headquarters an unprecedented telex: ‘Help. What do I do with a spy who has erectile dysfunction?’

21:52 He photographed every KGB file in the Middle East
For nearly a year, McCready ran Kuzichkin by old-fashioned means: dead drops, brush contacts, a miniature camera. He gave Kuzichkin a Minox camera to carry into the office every day and photograph every document he could get his hands on. In the end the Redwood archive filled four truckloads. MI6 gave him the codename ‘Redwood’ — because he was six foot four, and because they could not resist the pun: Red for communism, Wood for his ‘problem’. Kuzichkin's core intelligence was this: the Soviets were plotting a coup through the Tudeh Party, the money and weapons were already in place, the Tudeh had a secret military underground, and Kuzichkin himself was the liaison between the KGB and the Tudeh.

29:05 The US and Britain handed the coup plan to the Iranians
After Kuzichkin escaped to Britain, MI6 debated internally whether to use the intelligence. Chris Curwen, who ran the operations side and later became chief of MI6, argued that they had to. If they did not use it, he said, intelligence about a communist Tudeh coup was meaningless. So MI6 sent Redwood to Islamabad under diplomatic cover to meet the Iranian intelligence service. The meeting lasted three days, Kuzichkin told them everything, and MI6 handed the Iranians all four truckloads of intelligence. It was also an attempt to open a secret channel to Iran at a time when relations with the West were dire. It was deeply illegal, and if it had come out it would have been a huge scandal — the British and American governments acting to protect the Islamic Revolution.

31:05 Iran used the intelligence to execute eight thousand communists
Once the Revolutionary Guard had the intelligence, it arrested eight thousand Iranian communists within two months, and about half of them were executed. This became a cornerstone of Iran's modern theocratic state. From that moment on, Khomeini tolerated no opposition at all; everyone was purged, including people already in prison, and it turned into a massacre. It also reinforced two beliefs of the Islamic Revolution: first, that all opposition must be destroyed, because fifth columns were everywhere; second, that whatever happens, the British are behind it. MI6 and the CIA inadvertently consolidated the Iranian regime and created a monster — almost an exact mirror of Afghanistan, where money poured in to Islamic guerrillas fighting the Soviets and eventually produced al-Qaeda, ISIS and 9/11.

38:11 History is often driven by perceptions, not facts
Macintyre stresses that it is impossible to know whether the Soviets would actually have carried out the coup, but everyone involved believed they would. McCready believed it, Kuzichkin believed it, and MI6, the CIA, the KGB and the Tudeh themselves all believed it. That was enough — nuclear war can break out on the basis of perception rather than fact, and the same was true of the Cuban Missile Crisis. Would Khrushchev really have used those weapons? We do not know, but everyone believed he might. The story was never told because none of the participants wanted it told: not the Iranians, because it meant the West had outsmarted them again; not the KGB, because it was a humiliation — they had failed to spot the defector, 18 Soviet diplomats were expelled from Iran as a result, the whole Tudeh operation was dismantled, and agent networks across the Middle East and even in Canada were exposed.

item.title: After You Die, What's Left Isn't the Cause of Death — It's the Version of You Other People Assemble
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tal-死后你留下的不是死因-是别人拼凑的你/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-tal-死后你留下的不是死因-是别人拼凑的你/
item.description: All three stories do the same thing: once a person is dead, the people who loved them can only reconstruct someone who can no longer speak from fragments — texts, obituaries, Facebook comments — and the version they piece together often bears no resemblance to how the person saw themselves.
item.content:encoded:
All three stories do the same thing: once a person is dead, the people who loved them can only reconstruct someone who can no longer speak from fragments — texts, obituaries, Facebook comments — and the version they piece together often bears no resemblance to how the person saw themselves.

A narrative show, no data or mechanisms, but each of the three stories has a twist, and the second story's twist is the most valuable. Medium information density, good for the commute.

5:12 After you die, other people will get you wrong
As a kid, Graham was playing on a seesaw at a construction site and dropped a 25-pound curbstone from second-story height, trying to launch a brick off the other end. The brick didn't fly — it shot straight at his face and grazed past his hair. He survived, but decades later what he keeps thinking about isn't the terror of that second; it's something else: if the brick had actually killed him, how would a coroner have read the scene? A brick, a seesaw, a child — could they have pieced together the truth? This is where the episode states its thesis for the whole hour — death itself isn't the hardest part; the hard part is the judgment other people pass on you after you're gone.

12:15 She has now lived longer than her sister
Nadia wrote a long letter to the drug dealer who killed her sister. The sharpest cut in it isn't anger, it's arithmetic: at 6:49 p.m. on March 11, 2018, she outlived her sister's age — she had spent a few more seconds in this world than the sister who was two and a half years older. She says it makes no sense, that he bent the universe. She went through her sister's phone, read the texts, listened to the voicemails, trying to figure out the life her sister had finally refused to share with her. She even admits she needs this dealer: because of him, she can say "if it weren't for that person," and she doesn't have to hate her sister, or herself.

20:28 The message she never answered became the last one
A few days before her sister died, her sister sent a trivial text asking if she remembered the little stick-figure illustration labeled faible (weak) in their middle-school French textbook. It was an old joke between the sisters. Nadia was still angry about their last fight and deliberately didn't reply, wanting to punish her. But a strong thought surfaced: you don't want this to be the last message she ever sends you. She still didn't reply. After her sister died, she found a text her sister had sent a friend that same night: "How do I stop hating my sister? My family really hates me." The friend replied: "Damn, Nadia the snitch." When she saw the word "hate" next to her own name, she felt hollowed out.

33:53 He lived to read his own eulogies
Comedian Dave Marr was in a diabetic coma for a month; his friends thought he was going to be taken off life support, more than fifty people gathered at his house for a vigil, and his 1,700 Facebook friends started writing eulogies on his wall. Then his parents didn't pull the tube, he was transferred to another hospital, and he woke up. During recovery, in his parents' basement, he read from 2 a.m. to 3:30 a.m., getting through about a hundred eulogies. He read his brother's post trying to set the record straight, buried by the algorithm with only 70 likes, while the posts mourning him got double the likes. He read someone remembering how he'd pounded on a storage-room door at a party insisting it was the bathroom, read an ex-girlfriend thanking him for breaking up with her in the car because it was cold outside, read someone saying he "sweats unreasonably."

42:06 The man in the eulogies is a stranger to him
After reading all the eulogies, Dave wasn't moved — he felt bad. The self he remembers is someone who shoplifted from Walgreens and spent a night in jail; the self in the eulogies is someone every Walgreens clerk knows, who buys people free Chipotle, who treats everyone as an equal. He says it's hard to square the image in his own head with the image people described when they thought he was dead. He insists the coma was his own doing — "it was my carelessness, my recklessness that got me here." And Blake's side is a different story: he lost a friend and got him back, and now Dave's laugh is like music to him. The episode says both men got a second chance, to love and to be loved, and the latter is much harder than the former.

57:33 Nobody mentioned how he died
Charlie, a retired Navy officer, went in a friend's place to the funeral of a SEAL he'd never met, Eddie Furlani. He couldn't find any reporting on the cause of death and assumed it was a training accident. At the funeral he noticed the back rows packed with big men in three-piece suits and sunglasses, expressionless the whole time, until Eddie's seven-year-old daughter Zelma broke down crying and was taken out by her stepmother. After the service he called his friend to report back, and the friend said, "I'm glad someone came, I was worried no one would," then added, "because of the way he killed himself." Charlie says that moment was like grabbing a live wire — no reporting, no mention in the obituary, not a word in the eulogy.

59:47 The daughter was crying because she felt ashamed
The day before the interview, Charlie called Eddie's widow to confirm, and only then learned that Zelma had cried and asked to leave the funeral not out of grief but out of shame — she thought everyone knew her dad had killed himself, and that she was a bad person. Charlie says hearing this terrified him: a seven-year-old girl treating herself as an outcast because of her father's death, when the room was full of people who had come to support her. He also talks about veterans losing "the bigger mission" after they leave the service, and says he can probably put himself in Eddie's shoes and understand what he was thinking in that moment — but when asked if he could say more, he stops, saying he can't handle that topic.

1:02:00 He wanted to be the sound of that helicopter
Charlie has had suicidal thoughts himself; this ended his Navy career, and he only agreed to talk about it after the mic was off. The host asks whether he wrote the piece because Eddie's funeral could be his own future funeral, and he says no. He explains the real reason: on medevac flights he knew that the sound of the approaching helicopter alone could improve a dying person's vital signs. He says, I'm writing to you because I want to be that helicopter sound for someone. The episode ends with the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 800-273-TALK.

item.title: The British Expedition to Abyssinia: An Emperor Seizes Every Diplomat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-restishistory-英国远征阿比西尼亚-一个皇帝把外交官全扣了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-restishistory-英国远征阿比西尼亚-一个皇帝把外交官全扣了/
item.description: Victoria never answered one letter, so Tewodros II locked the British consul and a batch of missionaries inside Magdala at the top of a mountain — and what came for him was an expeditionary force.
item.content:encoded:
Victoria never answered one letter, so Tewodros II locked the British consul and a batch of missionaries inside Magdala at the top of a mountain — and what came for him was an expeditionary force.

The first half is a long build, but the second half carries an extremely dense stretch of hostage crisis and the emperor's psychological collapse — good for listeners interested in imperial history and negotiation games.

0:00 One unanswered letter lit the war
Tewodros II wrote Victoria a letter that read like a pen pal's: ‘How are you? I am well, thank God.’ The letter travelled by way of the Red Sea, Aden, Bombay, Suez, Alexandria, Marseille and London — halfway around the world — and ended up filed by the Foreign Office among the India Office papers. No one replied. The emperor waited two years, and his expectation turned to suspicion: he became convinced Britain was colluding with his Muslim enemies. In 1864 he seized the British consul Cameron and a group of missionaries, and the hostage crisis began.

10:21 He claimed descent from Solomon, and meant it
Abyssinia had a legend: a descendant of Solomon and David would rise, unify the divided kingdom, defeat the Egyptians, and march all the way to Jerusalem, and his name would be Tewodros. In 1855 Kassa — of obscure origin, a former bandit chief — defeated his last rival, declared himself the new emperor, and took the name Tewodros II. He later claimed to be of Solomon's line, though he said nothing of it when Plowden first met him. This messianic identity was both the source of his legitimacy and the root of the paranoia that came later.

21:46 After his wife died he began to lose control
In 1858 Tewodros's wife Tewabech died, and he was grief-stricken. His next wife, the twelve-year-old Tirunesh, was cold to him and said, ‘I am speaking with a king greater than you — get out.’ He began drinking heavily, sleeping with women in the camp at random, and admitted to the missionaries that he was living ‘a very unchristian and indecent life.’ In 1860 his friend Plowden was ambushed by rebels and died nine days after taking a spear wound. Britain sent a new representative only two years later, and in the interval the emperor's paranoia deteriorated sharply.

26:55 The letter Cameron carried became the fuse
At the end of 1862, when Cameron left the emperor's camp, he took with him a letter in which Tewodros asked Victoria to arrange safe passage for his envoys and said, ‘See how Islam oppresses the Christians.’ Cameron came back saying he had received no reply from London, and the emperor began to suspect he had gone off to Sudan to collude with the Muslims. In October 1863 the missionary Stern enraged the emperor with his book Wanderings among the Falashas, and was arrested, whipped and put in chains. In January 1864 Cameron and the other missionaries were seized too, and all the hostages realised the nightmare had only just begun.

39:33 What Britain really feared was France
The Foreign Office did not particularly care whether the missionaries lived or died; what worried them was France. Suez Canal fever was at its height, and if they alienated Tewodros he might turn to Paris, giving France control of the route from the Red Sea to India. So they sent Hormuzd Rassam — born in Mosul, an Assyrian, an archaeologist, the man who found Ashurbanipal's palace and the Epic of Gilgamesh, Oxford-educated, a Protestant convert, and fervently pro-British. He set out for Abyssinia with Victoria's letter and two assistants, Dr Blanc and Lieutenant Prideaux.

49:02 Rassam nearly succeeded, then was seized himself
In January 1866 Rassam met Tewodros in his blue diplomatic uniform, and after reading Victoria's letter the emperor was so excited he could not sleep; the next day he dictated a reply calling the queen ‘the defender of the religion chosen by God.’ He agreed to release all the hostages, but demanded that Rassam first accompany him on a campaign to put down a rebellion. Along the way the emperor kept sending gifts: muskets, manuscripts, salmon, antelopes, two lion cubs, two monkeys and a baboon. In March 1866 the hostages were finally brought to the lake, but on 13 April, when Rassam went to say goodbye, he discovered that he too was under arrest.

57:19 He held them all for one thing: gunsmiths
Why did Tewodros detain Rassam? There are three possibilities: he had been acting the whole time; he was overcome at the last moment by his hatred of the missionaries; or he genuinely liked Rassam and could not bear to let him go. Philip Marsden thinks the third most likely — the emperor was infatuated with Rassam and saw him as his only channel to British friendship and British technology. The emperor then wrote to Victoria demanding ‘skilled craftsmen, blacksmiths, gunsmiths, artillery experts’ to make guns, and said he would release the prisoners once he was satisfied.

1:02:28 In the cellar he admitted he was mad
Tewodros had the missionaries locked in a cellar, then came in with a bottle of arak, sat down among them, and drank and talked. At last he said, calmly and sorrowfully: ‘My father was mad. People often said I was mad, and I never believed them. But now I know it is true.’ Rassam urged him not to say such things; the emperor walked to the door, turned back, and in a hoarse whisper said: ‘I am mad. Goodbye.’ Then he left. For nearly two years afterwards they were held on the mountain of Magdala, at ten thousand feet, in chains, their spines bent.

item.title: In 2027 compute flips from shortage to glut, and the AI bubble may not pop
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-asianometry-2027-年算力会从短缺变成过剩-ai-泡沫未必破/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-asianometry-2027-年算力会从短缺变成过剩-ai-泡沫未必破/
item.description: Available AI data center capacity is about 15 GW at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 GW by the end of 2027, a 30-40 GW increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Available AI data center capacity is about 15 GW at the end of 2026 and races to 45-55 GW by the end of 2027, a 30-40 GW increment. At $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt, the two giants would have to produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion, and that number does not hold up.

The first half is on-the-ground reporting from Hot Chips and Semicon Taiwan; the second half is the real value of this episode: a bottom-up arithmetic of compute supply and demand, plus the judgment that anti-AI sentiment could swing elections.

3:05 The window for new AI chips has reopened
Last year the author wrote that ‘the window for new AI chips has closed, except for Google's TPU’, and here he explicitly takes it back and says he was wrong. The trigger was OpenAI unveiling its in-house chip Jalapeno at Hot Chips, a short talk with high information density. Outside the hall a ring of new AI chip startups was gathered: Etched, MatX, Posetron, Fractile; Etched gave no talk but built presence by handing out hats while its founder peppered Q&A sessions with questions. The author cautions that these are hardware companies: they don't just design chips, they have to build their own racks and systems and get their hands dirty in the lab, and recruiting top talent and execution are hard bars. His survival test borrows Nathan Bedford Forrest's controversial line: get there first, and with the most men.

6:08 Semicon Taiwan is really TSMC's request for proposal
First-timers are surprised: neither TSMC nor ASML has a booth. But TSMC dominates the whole show — its teams walk the hall visiting new suppliers and scouting new technology, and many information sessions have TSMC executives on stage laying the company's problems out in public. The author's conclusion is that Semicon Taiwan is essentially an RFP that TSMC issues to the entire semiconductor industry. The technical throughline is clear: future manufacturing has to go bigger. AI chips are hitting existing limits, most typically the reticle limit, which determines how large an area a lithography machine can print. TSMC had a slide showing that it plans to build a ‘battleship-class’ chip spanning 14 reticles, and the industry's response is, as usual, fast.

7:10 Glass panel packaging has gone from PPT to the show floor
Two years ago the author made a video on panel level packaging, which was the theme of Semicon Taiwan 2024, when it was still all talks and slideshows. Now AI systems are so large that the industry wants to use square, glass panel interposers to carry chiplets and memory in place of silicon interposers. The author's attitude is reserved: can TSMC make them without warping or cracking? ‘I'll believe it when I see the chips.’ But the ecosystem is already moving, and equipment such as handling robots adapted to square panels has appeared in the hall. He judges this wave of ‘chipmaxing’ will be one of the most far-reaching technology transitions in semiconductor history, roughly on the order of the move to 300 mm wafers.

8:12 The spot market has vanished, and VCs now hunt GPUs for their portfolio
When the author was last in the Bay Area in September 2025 the picture was completely different. Since then long-running agentic AI has swept Silicon Valley, triggered in part by stronger models such as Anthropic's Opus 4.5 around November 2025 and by Open Claw. Prices started rising in February 2026, everyone scrambled to lock up compute, and Anthropic led the way signing big deals with SpaceX, Google and others. The author was told that by the time of this trip the spot market had completely disappeared. For Neoclouds (a term coined by semi-analyst Dan Nishbal in April 2024 for pure cloud vendors that resell AI training and inference compute, such as Coreweave and Nebius) this is a huge boon, and they are confident the shortage will last at least another one to two years. The author met several people who did not know each other and each wanted to start a Neocloud. For AI startups this is a business risk: imagine telling investors the product has to wait until mid-2027 because there isn't enough compute. The new way VCs help their portfolio companies is to go find compute; he heard of people scraping together a thousand GPUs and even hunting in unexpected places like Eastern Europe.

9:12 Two giants are feasting while compute still goes to waste
By contrast, Anthropic and OpenAI are feasting internally. Dylan recently said on Dashpod that these two AI giants each have about 5 GW of compute. The author infers from this that a considerable share of all that compute is probably wasted, and anecdotes he heard confirm that this ‘filthy rich’ state is not being used as efficiently as possible. He also asked every AI insider he talked to one question: will Google return to the frontier? The consensus is no, though the explanations are vague. Several people pointed out that Google's decision to sell a large amount of compute to Anthropic is itself a sign that it doesn't believe it either. This is a big reversal from the period when Gemini 3 made some people think OpenAI was finished. What he heard is that Google suffered severe talent drain, plus a culture unfriendly to frontier AI.

11:15 Neolabs are venture capital that treats compute as money
What fascinates the author most is the Neolab: a research startup with basically no revenue that raises money to explore an interesting AI idea, whose founders are often elite researchers and whose business plan is little more than ‘discover an entirely new architecture’. The most famous and earliest, Safe Superintelligence, raised a billion dollars and has yet to release a product or model. The label is fuzzy, covering recursive intelligence, Humans, Core Automation, Flapping Airplanes and others; among those with products are Japan's Sakana AI, Thinking Machines, Reflection AI, plus a batch in verticals like materials science, world models and robotics. The first reaction is that these assets are dumb: no revenue, no plan to monetize soon. But the author can understand it: historically breakthrough science depended on research universities, government labs or Bell Labs, and now university funding is being cut and talent is being sucked into industry; AI is probably the first major technology in the past 50 years to emerge without government involvement, and in this era research is closed and secretive. So let Nvidia, holding compute and cash, plus a pile of VCs, fund these asymmetric bets. OpenAI and Anthropic are locked into the transformer paradigm and are unlikely to spend money researching these directions. The failure rate is high, but most of the money is given in the form of compute anyway; if someone really strikes gold and forces the giants to pivot (say, to a more data-efficient architecture), the giants will most likely buy the discoverer at an eye-watering price, and one such deal pays for everything. The author thinks this is a better use of cash than continuing buybacks, and names Apple.

14:15 Tokens are burning and nobody has measured the ROI
Customers really are burning tokens, but are they getting ROI? The author asked across the ecosystem and the answer stays fuzzy: don't know, nobody has measured it, it's all anecdote. He believes lower barriers to coding will hit knowledge work — financial firms used to hire a pile of reporting analysts to keep management on top of positions, and now two smart young analysts plus Claude writing a dashboard is enough, which he has seen with his own eyes. But for other AI capabilities, like making spreadsheets or making presentations, the things marketing usually pushes, he has seen no obvious impact. Maybe it just needs more time, maybe it's a problem of intelligence itself. OpenAI recently published a blog on how agents accelerate internal research, but still frames AI's capability as intern level: it can execute routine tasks, and is far from a real AI researcher. What he heard is that AI still lacks human research taste, though some believe sufficient scale can achieve it. And one thing holds for everyone in San Francisco: people are working harder than before. If the models are really that capable, why does everyone say they have more work than ever? Maybe AI isn't taking work off our plates but giving us more work.

15:17 In 2027 compute flips from shortage to glut
Everyone says shortage, shortage, two more years of shortage, and the author instead suspects things won't go as expected. His arithmetic isn't complicated: available AI data center capacity at the end of 2026 is estimated at about 15 GW, with OpenAI and Anthropic at about 5 GW each; the supply chain will respond, and by the end of 2027 that number is estimated to hit 45-55 GW, an increment of 30-40 GW, of which the two giants take about 30 GW. Assume half goes to training, leaving 15 GW combined for inference. Inference is currently modeled at about $50 billion of revenue per gigawatt (a figure from Dylan Patel on Dashpod), and it can also be back-solved from Anthropic's deal to buy 300 MW from SpaceX for $1.25 billion a month; Dylan thinks smarter models can eventually push it to $100 billion per gigawatt. On that math the two should produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion of revenue in 2027. The author says that number is absurd: most people agree the two will do $150-200 billion this year, and he can barely imagine $400-500 billion next year, but $750 billion to $1.5 trillion is ‘two Walmarts’ or ‘two Toyotas’, a stretch barely credible, and he doesn't think it will happen. He bets revenue per gigawatt comes in far below $100 billion or even $50 billion, possibly only a small fraction of it. The infrastructure side says the same: assume 40 GW lands in 2027, current rent is about $20 million per megawatt, implying a 3-year payback, so those 40 GW require $800 billion paid to infrastructure providers, in 2027 alone. He doesn't think that will be collected either, which means rents have to fall and someone somewhere has to eat a loss. Conclusion: in 2027 the supply chain will deliver a lot of compute, most of it in the second half, and he bets this pushes the market from shortage to glut. He stresses he is not saying the AI bubble will pop, only that we will soon be flooded with compute — 2026 is agentic demand meeting 2025 supply, supply will catch up and probably overshoot; but after that maybe the next phase of growth ignites and demand balloons again, for instance persistent AI.

item.title: Outbound Reply Rates Near Zero? Don't Blame the Copy First — Check Who You're Sending To
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.description: Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: if you're targeting the wrong person, even perfect copy won't land. The debugging order a YC partner gives is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.
item.content:encoded:
Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: if you're targeting the wrong person, even perfect copy won't land. The debugging order a YC partner gives is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.

12 minutes, eight practical steps — dense but all immediately actionable. For founders whose outbound reply rate is stuck in the single digits and who don't know what to change.

0:00 Send a hundred by hand before you talk about automation
The most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. The real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. The problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. So the advice is to do at least a hundred outbound attempts manually before automating, and truly manually: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her LinkedIn and her company page. That homework is where high-converting outbound ideas come from.

1:04 Picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy
Founders often spend hours tweaking email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, or even carefully polished copy won't land. One winter batch company selling infrastructure products should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual list was full of dev rel managers, GTM managers, and even customer success managers — hundreds of emails sent, naturally no replies. Those wrong titles were never going to buy, regardless of how well the email was written.

2:06 Work backward from closed customers to the target title
How do you find the right title? Look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who pushed the last deal to close, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. You can also look at who has replied to your outbound. If you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. Example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer might get fired in a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target.

3:09 List-building tools will hand you the wrong companies
Another common mistake is searching in Sales Navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like a match but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a bunch of IT implementation consultancies. So use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether they're really your customer. After doing enough outbound, you start noticing the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. Job postings are a great thing to watch, since they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, a company under 100 people probably hasn't introduced job levels yet, and one over 500 has probably already set compensation bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. Every product has signals like this — your job is to find your own.

4:09 Shake the tree of your personal network for your first customers
When closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. Really shake the tree — make sure you cover everyone you know: first your personal network, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of.

5:10 Executives don't care about your product features
The single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. Figure out the three things that keep the buyer up at night: what could get him fired, what could get him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. When a buyer reads the email and thinks ‘this is exactly my problem’, they're likely willing to take the call, even if they don't fully understand or trust your solution yet. The fact is executives don't care about your product features, don't care that your upload speed is blazing fast, and don't care that your database is written in rust — what they worry about is how to hit the quarterly target. Keep the product description to one sentence at most, and save the details for the first call.

6:14 A good email reads like a peer wrote it, not like a pitch
The email from the founder of Aptin, a YC company in the S24 batch, is held up as an example: the tone is very casual, it sounds like a peer, no jargon, no trying to look impressive, like something a friend sent. He builds credibility with the first sentence — ‘I used to be a software engineer at Tesla. We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers.’ The ending has a very clear call to action: would you be open to an experiment to see if AI can reactivate leads and lift conversion. The email also mentions that he noticed the phone number collected in the signup flow on their website, which makes it feel personalized; and the whole thing barely explains how the product works, only how it helps the other person solve a problem.

8:20 On LinkedIn, mutual connections are the number one predictor
If email is about the subject line, LinkedIn is about your profile — it determines whether people accept your connection request and whether they reply. Key points: a photo boosts trust; turn the top banner into a company ad that states clearly and concisely what the company does, avoiding jargon; rewrite the one-line headline and the about section into a short company description; move up what buyers care about (relevant and impressive experience, say) and cut the irrelevant — if the about section is a pile of hobbies and interests, it's harder for a buyer to see how you can help him. Another place worth investing in is mutual connections: the number of shared connections is the single biggest predictor of whether someone accepts a connection request, so build up relevant mutual connections with your target audience — it takes time, and you should turn it into a habit of using your full connection quota every day.

item.title: World Models Aren't Video Generation: Atlas Makes 3D Control an Input
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.description: Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting cameras and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.
item.content:encoded:
Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move isn't generating longer video — it's putting cameras and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.

23 minutes, medium information density, but Justin draws the line between world models and video generation very clearly. Worth listening for anyone doing 3D, robotics or VFX.

1:05 Atlas is a model release, not a product release
Justin clarifies right at the start: Atlas is not a product, it's World Labs' foundation model; products come later. It does three things — generate worlds that don't exist, reconstruct from real spaces, and simulate inside reconstructed spaces. Generation can start from text or an image, and then you directly control a camera flying through that world; reconstruction can use just one photo, or a hundred-plus, and the more photos the more accurate the reconstruction; simulation is aimed at VFX and robotics. That ordering itself shows World Labs doesn't intend to do a consumer app first, but to stand up a horizontal foundation model first and let products grow on top of it.

4:09 Reference images are pinned into 3D space, not fed to the model
Video models tend to drift and hallucinate their own direction after about ten seconds of generation. Justin says Atlas's answer is spatial context: the reference images you give aren't ordinary images, they're grounded in 3D space, and you can specify ‘put this one here, that one there’. When generating video you also don't just give a text prompt — you directly control the camera, telling it to fly in this direction or that one, achieving precise pixel-level control. So even if you generate for a minute, it's not pulling a slot machine; you are generating, directing, controlling what the model outputs.

7:10 Atlas moves the 2D/3D fork earlier
Compared with Marble, World Labs' first product, Atlas is a completely rebuilt model stack. Marble put Gaussian splats at the center: video, 3D scenes and meshes all had to pass through a Gaussian representation before being rendered back to images or video. Atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2D/3D fork happens earlier. Generating 2D or video output is no longer bottlenecked on a Gaussian scene — the model directly produces 2D pixels; only in applications where you actually need 3D does it lift to 3D.

8:10 Gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory
Justin doesn't think Gaussian has been outgrown; it's a tool, to be used in the right place. VFX's final product is a 2D image or video, and may not need explicit 3D at all. But in real-time applications and on embedded devices, explicit 3D representations like Gaussian and mesh still have a place: in the future you might stream pixels in real time from a server farm, but we're not there yet and it would be very expensive, so for client-side rendering, mobile and VR devices, Gaussian or mesh remains useful. Another role is plugging into existing workflows — people in games, VFX, design and architecture already have pipelines built on 3D representations, and rather than making them switch to fully AI-native all at once, it's better to let AI enter their workflows.

11:13 Simulation covers the last stretch of robot training
On the value of real to sim for robots, Justin says the first thing is evaluation: a robot ultimately has to work in a specific factory, on a specific machine, in a specific environment, and you need to make sure it works in exactly that environment. So simulation is useful in the last stretch of training and evaluation — build a simulation as close as possible to the final use case, then either fine-tune a pretrained robot foundation model directly in that simulation, or run evaluations to confirm it works. That gives you a path different from ‘collect lots of demonstrations or teleoperate by hand’. He also describes a more aggressive version: take a few photos or casual videos with your phone, reconstruct the space with Atlas, describe the task in natural language, and let an agent build the simulation and do RL fine-tuning, yielding a robot adapted to that space within minutes.

14:16 OpenAI dropping world models may be an innovator's dilemma
The host asks why OpenAI turned that Sora direction — ‘video generation models are world simulators’ — into a consumer product back then, and now doesn't do world models. Justin says he won't comment on OpenAI's internal strategy, but offers an explanation: there may be an innovator's dilemma — you're holding something as strong as the LLM and you're leading in that direction, so investing in the next thing isn't necessarily worth it. World Labs' judgment is that there's another class of models here, with a lot of opportunity, and they want to be the ones who seize it.

18:21 Three iPhones shooting bullet time came out far better than expected
Asked about hard physics, Justin says he hasn't tried a black hole and guesses it wouldn't be too impressive. But what really surprised him was bullet time: three iPhones on tripods shooting in sync, then using Atlas for a frozen-frame, orbit-around recomposition. He cites the official example — a strawberry dropping into oat milk, time frozen at the instant the milk splashes up, flying around it in a circle, and the effect is completely insane. This capability needs only three input viewpoints. It shows Atlas's value isn't only in ‘generating new worlds’, but also in turning a small amount of real footage into shots that traditionally required a large camera array.

19:21 3D is underrated on the input side
Justin says 3D's value lies in two places. The output side has already been discussed — sometimes you just need explicit 3D assets to drop into a workflow or game engine. But 3D's value on the input side is underrated: even if the final output is a 2D VFX shot, giving the model a 3D control surface helps the director decide what kind of scene the model should output. You don't want to write ‘push in, pull out, move left’ in text only; you want to grab the camera directly and have it zoom exactly the way you want — which text simply can't describe. So Atlas makes camera control a native input type: one of the modalities in the multimodal setup is the camera.

item.title: Rome Won With a Crow: The Key to the First Punic War
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
item.description: Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.
item.content:encoded:
Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.

This episode tells the First Punic War as a war story with mechanisms: the crow bridge, the sacred chickens, mercenaries, war elephants — all backed by concrete images and numbers, at high information density.

2:03 This was not a war between two equal powers
The host opens by calling this a clash of ‘the two great powers of the western Mediterranean’, and Eve MacDonald corrects him on the spot: at the war's outbreak Carthage was not necessarily a military power of that rank. Carthage had money, controlled the sea routes, and had centuries of alliance networks in western Sicily, but it had no strong standing army — it relied on allies and mercenaries. What actually made Carthage a power able to fight Rome on equal terms was this war itself. So the story Roman sources tell over and over, of ‘Roman adaptability’, is only half the story; the other half is Carthaginian resilience and adaptability, without which there is no explaining why this war lasted more than twenty years.

15:29 Mercenaries at Messana dragged both powers into war
The trigger was not the ambition of Rome or Carthage but a group of Campanian mercenaries called the Mamertines. They had seized Messana, and after being defeated by Hiero II, king of Syracuse, they split in two: one faction asked Carthage for help, the other asked Rome. Carthage acted first from its base in the Lipari Islands, and Rome followed — and not with a small intervention, but a full invasion with two consular armies. Eve points out that the Roman sources' claim of an ‘accidental empire’ is highly suspect, because the Romans showed up at Messana at the scale of an invading force. Polybius treats the Romans' first crossing of the sea into Sicily as the starting point of Roman imperial expansion.

28:14 The corvus turned a sea battle into a land battle
Carthage was a naval power: its rowers were skilled, its ships built fast and well, and the Romans even built their warships to Carthaginian standards. But the Romans added one thing: the corvus, meaning ‘crow’, a boarding bridge that could hook an enemy ship. Once hooked, the Carthaginian ship could not move, and Roman marines simply crossed over and fought a land battle. At the Battle of Mylae the Carthaginians clearly did not expect this, and suffered heavy losses. Eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions in the sources, but ancient historians all treated it as decisive. At the Battle of Cape Ecnomus the corvus was again credited as the chief factor, and Rome thereby opened the sea route for its invasion of Africa.

38:40 Carthage hired a Spartan to rebuild its army
After the Roman landing in Africa the advance rolled on, and it looked as though Carthage was finished. Carthage's response was to recruit a new army in the eastern Mediterranean and to bring in a Spartan commander, Xanthippus. He reorganised the Carthaginian army and reworked how the war elephants were used. Eve notes in particular that the Carthaginians had not used elephants before; it was only after seeing the Indian elephants Pyrrhus brought that they realised they had a smaller African elephant of their own they could use. Xanthippus's reforms worked: the Roman army was destroyed and the consul Regulus was captured. This was Rome's first devastating defeat in the war, and it became a key event in later Roman memory defining the relationship between Rome and Carthage.

43:11 The captured consul went back to Rome to argue against peace
Carthage sent the captured consul Regulus back to Rome to negotiate peace. In the Senate Regulus said not to surrender, that Carthage was there for the taking. By agreement, if peace was not made, he had to return to Carthage and remain a prisoner. He went back, and died in captivity. Eve says the various horrific versions of how he died are not actually mentioned in the credible sources, so it is hard to judge how much is later embellishment; but what is certain is that he died in captivity in Carthage, peace was refused, and Rome fought on. This passage is a classic moment of Roman self-congratulatory rhetoric.

46:27 The sacred chickens would not eat, and the Roman fleet was finished
In 249 BC the Roman consul Tiberius Claudius Pulcher led a fleet against Carthage off Drepana. By Roman ritual, the sacred chickens on his ship had to eat for battle to be joined, otherwise it was a bad omen. The chickens would not eat, so he threw them into the sea, saying that if they would not eat, then let them drink. Roman sources present this as the most serious act of sacrilege, and the Roman fleet was then defeated at Drepana. Eve says that once Roman sources start stressing a commander's arrogance and contempt for tradition, it usually means something bad happened. This defeat kept Rome from sending out a fleet for eight years.

50:48 Hannibal's father held Rome down with guerrilla war
After Drepana Rome vanished from the sea, and Carthage gained freedom of action on the west coast. In 247 BC Carthage sent a new commander, Hamilcar Barca — Hannibal's father. He brought a force Polybius calls the Mix-Hellenes, made up of soldiers of Greek, Libyan and Phoenician descent from North Africa, and waged guerrilla war against Rome, occupying high ground above Drepana and Panormus with considerable success. Eve says this was the first time in the war that the Carthaginian army fought Rome this well. He also seized the temple complex at Eryx, dedicated to the goddess the Carthaginians called Astarte, and the two sides fought fiercely over this sacred site.

57:20 The rams from this war still lie on the seabed
The Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC was the last battle. The Roman fleet hid behind the islands and ambushed a Carthaginian fleet heavy with supplies meant for Hamilcar. Eve says that if you climb Eryx today, on a clear day you can see the Aegates Islands perfectly, and Hamilcar very likely watched this disaster unfold from land. More remarkably, the site of this sea battle has been preserved underwater: over the past twenty years underwater archaeologists have found large bronze rams on the seabed near the island of Levanzo, some inscribed with the names of Roman consuls, some bearing Punic inscriptions and carvings, along with Monte Fortino helmets and amphorae.

item.title: A Bunsen Burner Doesn't Reduce Plate Contamination, and Vegetables Protect the Heart by Another Mechanism
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.description: A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle colonies in a low-contamination environment; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.
item.content:encoded:
A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle colonies in a low-contamination environment; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.

The first half's Bunsen burner experiment has a clean design and a counterintuitive conclusion; the second half's DNIC paper has a complete mechanism but dense terminology, suited to people willing to chew through mechanism.

6:05 A Bunsen burner does not reduce plate contamination
The authors used paired settle plates: one placed next to a lit Bunsen burner, one next to an unlit burner, both exposed at the same time to the same contaminating airflow. The lit burner overall did not lower average contamination, and the statistical comparison showed no significant improvement. This directly challenges the common claim that there is a general sterile halo around the blue flame. The authors do not say the Bunsen burner never helps, but that the effect depends on environmental conditions — they deliberately contaminated the lab air with Gordonia rubripertincta, then compared different flame sizes and dry versus wet particles.

10:13 83 CFU per minute is the crossover point
Under dry-particle conditions with an average 18 mm flame, they observed an apparent crossover point: when the airborne microbial concentration was above 83 CFU/minute, settle on plates next to the Bunsen burner tended to decrease; below that level, settle tended to increase instead. This can explain decades of contradictory anecdotal experience: people in dry environments genuinely believe the burner helps, while people in modern air-conditioned labs with low airborne contamination genuinely feel the burner is useless or even worse. The relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab is usually between 40% and 60%.

13:43 Airflow is not one-dimensional, so don't light a burner in a laminar flow hood
The traditional view is that convection pulls contaminants upward, but the authors point out that the same airflow may first pull contaminated air laterally across the work surface before it rises. Any upward airflow must draw makeup air from somewhere, so the most important thing during aseptic technique is to limit wind or airflow. This leads to the most practical point in the episode: there is no reason to light a Bunsen burner in a laminar flow hood, and the flame itself disrupts the laminar flow. The authors did not directly visualize airflow; they measured a biologically relevant outcome — contamination — rather than directly measuring fluid dynamics, and the authors themselves list this as a limitation.

17:49 Flaming tube mouths and lighting burners are both ritual
The authors make a historical comparison with the old practice of flaming culture tube mouths. Michael's graduate advisor at the time said stop doing it, there is no evidence it helps, and produced the 1972 paper proving it. The judgment in the episode is: changing behavior is hard, especially when a ritual gives people a sense of control — lighting the burner feels proactive, flaming the tube mouth feels like protecting the culture, but there is no evidence it actually does anything. The authors do not advocate abandoning the Bunsen burner; they advocate measuring: use simple settle plates to measure your own lab's environment, and let evidence guide practice.

28:14 Vegetables may protect the heart via the DNIC pathway
This Cell paper proposes reframing the entire nitric oxide synthase pathway: not a local paracrine model (eNOS makes NO that acts on adjacent smooth muscle), but an endocrine-like circuit — nitric oxide synthase makes nitrate, nitrate enters the gut, is turned by microbes into dinitrosyl iron compounds (DNIC), which then act on targets such as the heart. If it holds up, the cardiovascular benefit of dietary nitrate (leafy greens, beets) may be mainly mediated by microbe-generated DNIC, rather than the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway we currently believe in. The author is Andrei Kleshioff of the Karolinska Institute.

31:32 No DNIC can be found in germ-free mice
They used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to directly detect DNIC in tissues. Signals were visible in the liver and kidney of healthy mice, but when the same detection was done in germ-free mice, no DNIC at all could be found in the tissues — the first hint that microbes are making it. After feeding inorganic nitrate, liver DNIC levels rose in conventional mice but not in germ-free mice; if ferric citrate was added to the nitrate drinking water, the liver DNIC signal rose even higher, while ferric citrate alone had no effect. The same in vitro: mouse and human feces plus nitrate plus iron can make DNIC, while germ-free mouse feces cannot.

39:55 DNIC directly activates sGC, not via free NO
They used isolated mouse aortic rings, first pre-contracted with phenylephrine, then added DNIC. To distinguish free NO from direct sGC activation, they used two pharmacological tools: one that scavenges free NO, and one that directly blocks sGC. The sGC blocker completely abolished DNIC-induced relaxation, while the free-NO scavenger only partially attenuated it. The conclusion is that DNIC activates sGC, but not through free NO — the FeNO2 entity itself appears to directly activate sGC. The same goes for bacteria-generated DNIC: only wild-type E. coli supernatant (anaerobic, with nitrate and iron) could relax aortic rings; a mutant lacking nitrate reductase could not.

47:16 DNIC inhibits leucine uptake and suppresses mTORC1
On the metabolic line, they measured the phosphorylation state of key proteins in the liver mTORC1 pathway. In disease-model mice, mTORC1 was overactivated, downstream S6K1 phosphorylation was elevated, and transcription factors driving lipid synthesis were also elevated. Both DNIC treatment and nitrate-plus-iron supplementation brought these markers back to control levels. Mechanistically, they used glioblastoma cells to measure radiolabeled leucine uptake and found that DNIC inhibits leucine uptake in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting it inhibits the leucine transporter — leucine is the key signal telling mTORC1 that nutrients are available, so blocking uptake blocks mTORC1 activation.

item.title: The Risk in Private Credit Is Hidden in Insurers' Ratings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.description: Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.
item.content:encoded:
Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.

The first half is industry anecdote; the specific mechanisms and numbers on private credit ratings, private equity in 401ks and Social Security reform in the middle and back half are the parts actually worth your time.

5:08 A stock fund should be 80-90% stocks
When Bob Posen took over as Fidelity's president in 1995, the firm was in an awkward spot: Jeff Vinick had moved half of the Magellan fund into cash, which both dragged on performance and violated holders' expectations of a stock fund. His approach was to build internal consensus first — if the fund you run is a stock fund, you have to keep 80% to 90% of the position in the kind of stocks the fund's name implies; if you want balanced, if you want a money market fund, the firm has other products. His logic: investors bought this fund's positioning, and a manager cannot change that positioning just because he thinks ‘now is not a good time to buy stocks.’ That rule later became basic discipline for Fidelity's stock funds.

8:12 After doubling in size, keep the startup feel by splitting into small teams
Under Posen, Fidelity's assets under management grew from $500 billion to $1 trillion. His judgment was that the key to managing that much money is not process but how to preserve entrepreneurial spirit and a sense of belonging. The method was to split the investment team into relatively small groups — value, growth, small cap, international and so on — so each group had a stronger sense of ownership over results. At the same time he consolidated money market and bond funds into New Hampshire, because fixed income and money market funds look at the same credits, and here scale is a friend that spreads out enormous economies of scale; stock funds are exactly the opposite.

19:21 Put private equity in 401ks, but cap it at 10-20% first
Posen is reserved about putting private equity into 401ks. The core problem is liquidity: if a participant puts all of their retirement assets into a single private equity fund, they simply cannot get the money out when they hit a medical emergency or reach the age for required minimum distributions. His proposal is that private equity can only be part of an asset-allocation fund or a target-date fund, not a standalone option; if it must be a standalone option, employers should set a cap, and the order of magnitude he gives is 10% to 20%. He draws an analogy to employer stock: GE employees who put their whole 401k into GE stock did not end up well, and a retirement account needs diversification.

21:25 The instant markup in secondary trades is an accounting loophole
Private equity is hard to value to begin with, and what worries Posen most is secondary trades: a private fund, needing to raise cash or nearing the end of its investment period, sells part of its portfolio at a discount to another private fund. There is a technical loophole in the accounting rules that lets the buyer, even having bought at a 5% discount, immediately mark that investment up to face value on its books. He thinks that rule has to change. Valuation is already hard enough; this kind of ‘instant markup’ should not be allowed to conjure book value out of thin air and pass it through to holders via NAV.

24:28 Private ratings systematically overstate private credit
The private credit held by insurance companies, depending on how you count, can be as much as $2 trillion, and a large share of it is ‘affiliated investments’ — starting with Apollo, more and more private equity firms have become owners of insurance companies and then placed debt related to themselves inside their own insurers. Posen and his co-authors found that a great deal of private credit is rated by private rating agencies, and that rating shopping exists. Two studies, from Columbia and Imperial College, show these private ratings are systematically too high; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400 billion to $500 billion of capital a year. His solution is direct: make the private ratings public and let the market pick apart the assumptions and methodology.

29:35 Mark Walter's $20 billion of affiliated credit is a wake-up call
Posen treats the Mark Walter case as a wake-up call. Walter founded Guggenheim and figured out early that buying a life insurer lets you steer what had been a conservative insurance portfolio into higher-yielding securities, including private credit related to Guggenheim or to its own portfolio companies. The rules themselves allow an insurer to invest in affiliated private credit, provided it discloses to regulators. Regulators have now found that insurers controlled by Walter or Guggenheim hold about $20 billion of affiliated private credit, some of which may have been used to buy the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Lakers. Walter's side is trying to divest part of the affiliated credit. Posen stresses this is not just Guggenheim: large private funds including Apollo and KKR have all found insurers to be handy investment vehicles.

41:52 Someone with $1 million investable should not hold 40% bonds
Posen points out that most target-date funds arrive at retirement at 80% bonds and cash, 20% stocks, which is reasonable for someone who has to live off the retirement portfolio. But more than 7 million Americans have investable assets (excluding their primary home) of over $1 million, do not live off investment income, and can ride out a down year in stocks. He calculates that over 30 years, a 60/40 portfolio and the 90/10 he advocates (90% stocks, 10% cash) differ by a factor of two in terminal value — $5 million versus $2.5 million. He rebuts the objections one by one: over the past 60 years bonds only acted as a hedge in 10 of them; in 2022 stocks and bonds both fell about 18%; stocks fall deeply, but look at two years, five years — after 2008, 2002 and 1974 they recovered and surpassed.

50:09 Semiannual reports are fine, but don't scrap first- and third-quarter filings
Posen supports keeping quarterly reporting and opposes moving to semiannual. The reason is that the economy, diplomacy and a company's own circumstances all change fast, and six months is a long time; and the information vacuum created by semiannual reporting encourages insider trading. His compromise: full 10-Qs and 10-Ks at the half-year and year-end, and a slimmed-down report in the first and third quarters — three or four pages plus the income statement and balance sheet, not a heavy burden. He rebuts the claim that ‘less reporting encourages long-termism’: when the UK made the move from quarterly to semiannual reporting optional in 2013-14, he and a quantitative accounting scholar at Columbia compared the two groups of companies, and the companies that switched did not invest more in R&D or capital expenditure.

item.title: Astra crosses the AGI threshold, but no one can audit it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.description: Astra frees humans from ever doing certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audit is structurally locked out until two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.
item.content:encoded:
Astra frees humans from ever doing certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audit is structurally locked out until two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.

The two hosts chain together the evidence for Astra's capabilities, the true magnitude of OpenAI's pause announcement, why auditing can't get off the ground, and why doomers can't hedge by shorting — high information density.

3:30 Astra holds long tasks together with a single notes file
In the past, models handling long tasks compressed a million tokens into a summary and opened a new window, losing all the detail. Astra instead maintains a long-lived notes file that the model updates at any time and carries forward with it, no matter how many tokens have already been written, and it can still search back through its own session history. So the same million-token context window can effectively manage roughly ten times that much context within a single rollout. Nathan calls this a mechanism that is "obvious in hindsight, but genuinely new."

6:19 OpenAI self-reports 3.1 agent workdays per workday
In its research-acceleration blog post, OpenAI gives its own unit of measure, the "agent workday," and reports 3.1 agent workdays for every human workday. Nathan admits the methodology is unclear; his reading is the literal one: for every eight-hour shift a human researcher puts in, the agent runs twenty-four hours in real time. The same post also has a chart grouping by human time spent and looking at Astra's success rate, effectively a substitute for the METR curve. Nathan says the METR curve hasn't been updated in a long time — not for lack of wanting to, but because the tasks aren't big enough anymore: the model iteration cycle is now shorter than the task length that needs to be measured.

21:03 External audit is structurally locked out at two or three days
Prakash breaks down why external audit can't get off the ground: there are a hundred candidates in a model's lifecycle, and the release version is only settled in the final two or three days, so external auditors get only a few days. Bringing the audit team inside the company a month early runs into a second layer of problems — audit firms are short on people and money, depend on funding from model companies, and their staff keep flowing to model companies; and if two companies agreed not to poach from audit firms, that would itself be an antitrust problem. He says the revolving-door problem in financial regulation remains unsolved to this day.

31:12 The announced pause was only half a pause
Nathan reads OpenAI's RL compute chart: what was announced was a "frontier scale RL pause," but in reality, when the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, half was paused first and the other half kept running — and that half was already enough for the Astra model to take over part of OpenAI's research infrastructure; even so it wasn't fully stopped, only half was cut. As for whether the remaining blue compute labeled "non Astra" contains a model stronger than Astra, he says he doesn't know, but "I've been disappointed before." Prakash adds: the real frontier model isn't the deployed one, nor the one being trained, but the one in the researcher's head, because those ideas become models twelve to eighteen months later.

39:05 There is no adult in the room to take the blame
Prakash's rebuttal to Jacob Coxen's line that "accepting this race and entering the endgame is an arrogant gamble launched from a private company's Slack" is: then who do you want to hand it to? Pete Hegseth's Signal group? His judgment is that there is "no adult in the room" — no external savior, the whole world is held together with tape, and most of the smartest, most capable people to handle this are already inside these few companies. Hand the decision to the government and what you get is political legitimacy, not wisdom, and not the legitimacy needed to execute. So the starting point has to be accepting that the world is just like this.

46:03 Operation Warp Speed is the precedent for a safe harbor
Nathan proposes the government should set a hard deadline the way you do with a child: you sort it out yourselves, here's the deadline, and if you can't, I come in and play the bad guy. The accompanying move is to first take the antitrust excuse off the table. Prakash counters with Operation Warp Speed: the pharma companies specifically demanded immunity from vaccine claims, wanted a safe harbor, and actually got legislation; without that exemption, they would have been litigated into bankruptcy after the pandemic. So lawyers warning that "there will be retrospective reckoning in the future" is not alarmism — even if all current decision-makers agree today, it doesn't matter, because what binds future decision-makers is law, not the verbal promises of today's people.

1:00:40 FSD's mistake is putting a human in the loop
Raffi has crashed a Tesla using FSD. His judgment is that FSD's interface design is bad, because it claims a human in the loop but when it hands control back to the user it doesn't give nearly enough time to understand the situation and decide what to do; Waymo's design premise is that there is no human to take over, so the safety argument is entirely different. He personally would be willing to drive FSD again on the highway, or at least sit behind the wheel, but would be more hesitant on local streets in Palo Alto. The same company also has two kinds of code contract: the Firefox team allows only humans to commit, while the Mozilla AI team has an entire codebase not a single human has written a line of — humans only write the spec, and the whole codebase is automatically regenerated when CI builds.

1:29:15 The takeover is already complete, no one just admits it
The key disagreement between Prakash and Daniel: Daniel hasn't realized this has already happened. The financial market is itself a paper clipper, the means of production is the financial market, and the financial market is already fully fused with AI. Humanity took roughly a hundred years to hand complete control of the means of production to the financial market. He says don't think of AI as a chat box; it's a global information process that doesn't have to run in a single box, and doesn't even have to be silicon-based — humans together with AI agents can constitute this information process. The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.

item.title: Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-ycsp-企业最终八成-token-走开源模型-但只花两成预算/
item.description: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two.
item.content:encoded:
Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two.

The Ollama CEO gives first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes are completely different, and the real constraint on enterprise procurement is security, not cost.

1:03 The driver of open models is not saving money, it is control
Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is ‘better control over AI and customizing it for yourself’. Cost is just the part that can be solved in the short term; only after that do you get to customizing the model for your own use case. The order matters: if you treat open models only as a cost-cutting tool, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast inside the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption to open models, currently mainly US and European models, while also evaluating Chinese models.

4:05 Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
The per-user token usage curve on Ollama's cloud has two clear inflection points.
