The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could support a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, customer service, marketing and sales can all throw a hard problem at an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and fetching data along the way, consuming enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million is the technical precondition for this explosion.

8:08 Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors before launch, but Jeff says getting a model a few weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work is crammed into the final 24 hours before release. Three things have to be done at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, to make sure it is fast, accurate and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are now many open-source harnesses like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the biggest growth day. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, inference layer and application runtime all have to be glued together, a combinatorial explosion problem.

14:11 The new scarcity is what sits above the token
Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (connecting company data and context to the model), coordination (one request spawns a pile of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, that need scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgment: tokens are already in oversupply, dozens of open model providers can supply them, and what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B above the token. Following the path of cloud computing, developers will ultimately prefer the best standalone product at every layer rather than a packaged Heroku or Google App Engine.

17:14 Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
Asked whether the harness will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgment is that the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but several categories cannot. First, state — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge independent problem space. Second, credential management and security. Open models do not come with a full set of security tooling the way closed providers do, and that is critical for enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

18:15 80% of tokens go through open models, but only 20% of budget
Jeff's steady-state judgment: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will go through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget flows to open models. The open community is driving costs extremely low, so maybe only 10% to 20% of spending lands on open models. The hardest work stays with frontier labs, because that is where the best researchers are; the broad middle is done by combining open and closed models. He uses a law firm analogy: partners hand work down to a bunch of associates.

22:19 Local and cloud model mixes are completely different
On local models, US and Chinese models are basically neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a mix of US, European and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is also clear: coding agents write code and tests, with many hard problems, mainly relying on large cloud models; document processing and other end-to-end low-difficulty workflows run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, plus a router deciding when to go up to a large model.

29:25 The Flash tier is the precondition for unlimited tokens
Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, less than 3 months behind the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve was extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually return to that state, but it requires model architectures specifically trained for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.

item.title: One Report Closed Over a Hundred Medical Schools, and Black Doctors Were Cut Off for Decades
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-stuffmissed-一份报告关掉上百所医学院-黑人医生从此断层/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: The Flexner Report is often written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years no new Black medical school appeared.
item.content:encoded:
The Flexner Report is often written up as the starting point of modern medical education, but it also closed five of seven Black medical schools, and for nearly forty years no new Black medical school appeared.

Medium information density. The first half is a chronological slog through Flexner's life; the real value is in the second half — how the report reshaped medical education, and how it cut off the supply of Black doctors.

6:09 The report's author was not a doctor but an education reformer
Abraham Flexner was not a medical man. In 1890 he ran an experimental school with no fixed curriculum, no exams and no grades, and its students still got into good schools; in 1908 he wrote The American College, A Criticism, attacking American higher education, which is why Henry Smith Pritchett of the Carnegie Foundation came to him and asked him to turn the same critical eye on the medical schools of the United States and Canada. He spent two years travelling to 155 medical schools, recording each one's admission requirements, faculty, finances, laboratories and hospital affiliations, and in 1910 delivered Medical Education in the United States and Canada. It was precisely because he was an outsider rather than a member of the medical community that the assessment dared to be so unsparing.

14:23 Medical schools were still teaching out-of-date knowledge
In the fifty years before the report, bacteriology, diagnostic technique and surgery were all changing fast, but medical schools had no uniform standards. At many schools the faculty were practising physicians who taught the way they themselves had been taught and did not update the content. The result was that the care the doctors they produced gave patients was, at best, antiquated and, at worst, life-threatening. Admission standards were just as chaotic: when the report was published, 74% of medical schools required only a high school diploma, some accepted even a high school equivalency certificate, only one in five required more than two years of college coursework, and many schools were essentially for-profit businesses.

18:31 He recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools
Flexner set standards first and then graded school by school: admission should require college-level biology, chemistry and physics; the curriculum should include classroom and laboratory work in anatomy, pathology, bacteriology and pharmacology; there should be a teaching hospital for hands-on practice; and teachers should be salaried, full-time teaching and research staff rather than practising physicians doing this on the side. He published the results by state and by school, naming dirty laboratories and lax standards, and criticising course schedules that left students sitting for hours, exhausted, listening to dull lectures by part-time teachers. In the end he recommended closing 120 of the 155 schools. Within a decade the number of American medical schools was down to half; the schools that survived reformed their standards and curricula, and laboratory and clinical teaching were modernised substantially. In Canada only one school made the closure list, and it ultimately did not close.

23:43 He never did the arithmetic on Black medical schools' books
The report was equally unsparing toward Black medical schools, saying that five of the seven "can make no valuable contribution at this moment", and affirming only Howard and Meharry as worth developing. But the assessment did not take into account that Black medical schools charged far less in tuition than white schools, had smaller endowments, and were already running on extremely thin margins. He wrote that "the Negro needs good schools rather than many schools", and said that one of the most important duties of Black people and Black nurses was to teach hygiene rather than life-saving skills — a sentence that is itself racist. Every Black medical school he named as inadequate closed: the first four before 1914, the fifth in 1915, and the last held on until 1923.

25:48 The next Black medical school would not come until 1966
Howard and Meharry survived and are still there today. But the next medical school primarily serving Black students was Charles R. Drew Medical School in Los Angeles, which did not open until 1966, and then in response to the Black community's need for access to care; the one after that was Morehouse School of Medicine in Atlanta in 1975. The direct consequence of narrowing the options was a huge care gap: many potential doctors were shut out of educational opportunity by geography, and Black patients were often cared for by white doctors who, even at best, carried inherent racial bias. An expert panel convened by the AMA's Institute for Ethics in 2005 concluded that Flexner's line about "good schools rather than many schools" ensured that medicine remained segregated, and that the communities that most needed doctors were the ones left without them.

26:51 The AMA was paying behind Carnegie's project
One fact not disclosed at the time: the Carnegie Foundation hired Flexner for this project, and the AMA was also a sponsor. There is also an unresolved question — whether someone connected to the AMA accompanied him on some of the school visits. His accounts differed at different times: sometimes he said the man went with him, later he changed his story to say they merely met there, so whether the report was subject to more direct directional influence cannot be determined to this day.

28:53 Did he know he was constraining Black medicine?
He knew. The report contains a passage of idealistic colour, saying that building up Howard and Meharry would benefit the nation far more than barely sustaining more schools. In 1933 he wrote to the board of the institute he had founded, arguing that hiring and admissions "shall not directly or indirectly take race, religion or sex into account". One explanation comes from his biographer Thomas Neville Bonner: when Flexner was growing up in Louisville, the local Black community had more services and opportunities than in many places, with a dozen or so Black schools and vocational training in medicine and law for Black students; the Flexners were not well off, there were Black families among their neighbours, and he and his siblings often played with Black children in the community. This may have left him overly idealistic about the reality of Black family life, and he later admitted that it was not until he began studying educational institutions that he realised how disadvantaged those Black classmates of his had been.

35:01 The hygiene line may not have been his own
The claim that hygiene was the main duty of Black doctors is one of the key pieces of evidence for calling Flexner racist. But the leaders of Meharry and Howard had said similar things in 1907 and 1908 — two or three years before the report — and those leaders were also white. This suggests Flexner's formulation may have been a restatement of the schools' established mission rather than a judgement he reached independently. In 2011 Lynn E. Miller and Richard M. Weiss, writing in the Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences, proposed another possibility: that this language was in fact opening up a public health role for the doctors at these schools, in order to win support across racial divisions — because those statements about hygiene being the most urgent need were immediately followed by the conclusion that these institutions obviously ought to be supported. In 2008 the AMA issued a public apology for its history of racial inequality.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Nested Loops, but Loops Only Climb to Local Optima
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-a16z-公司正在变成一串嵌套的-loop-但-loop-只能爬到局部最优/
item.description: After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. Loops help you climb to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.
item.content:encoded:
After prompt comes agent, after agent comes loop. Loops help you climb to a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain.

Anish ties together agent deployment, model pricing, and consumer AI bottlenecks into one thread, and the second half's judgments on moats and product problems are worth more than the first half.

0:00 Ideas that are too small no one will fund now
Anish says that three years ago, if a company wanted to do something too grand, a16z would not invest; today it is the opposite—they do not want to touch ideas that are too small or too local. The reason is that model capabilities have removed the threshold of "can it be done," and the remaining constraint is ambition itself. He calls this technology "unbundling skill from desire": not only can productivity be amplified, but the scale of what you want to do can be amplified as well.

6:10 It is not recursive self-improvement, it is autocatalytic
Anish rebuts the "fast takeoff" narrative: the people who understand it best in the labs are not talking about RSI (recursive self-improvement) but about autocatalytic effects—using new technology to improve your own processes, but not truly recursively. He gives two counterexamples: first, economic diffusion is extremely slow; when he went back to his hometown, he found people's lives had not changed much; second, many problems are not intelligence bound at all—give FedEx or Domino's a data center full of PhDs, and it will not make supply chains and pizza exponentially crush the competition.

8:16 Using AI and reorganizing around AI are two different things
Anish uses the diffusion of electricity as an analogy: from the invention of electricity to the actual reorganization of factories took 40 years, and it meant burning down old factories and rebuilding, not swapping coal for electricity. Today the most aggressive companies redesign everything around models, while slower companies just grant permissions to existing roles and functions. He also gives the example of the Mexican used-car company Kavak's Jedi Academy: a six-week course teaching everyone, including mechanics, to use new tools, and at graduation each person delivers an agent in a production environment.

11:18 Companies will become a series of nested loops
Anish's steel man: after prompt comes agent (a loop of model plus tools, memory, and skill files), after agent comes loop (a group of agents doing tasks). Coding got there first because the models are best, the users are the most technical, and there is already a mature loop—bug reports come in, generate a reproduction, fix it, high-risk changes get human confirmation, low-risk ones go straight to production, and even automatically reply to the customer. Above that there are loop per person, loop per job function, loops across business units, up to a loop that can run most of the company.

14:18 Loops only climb to a local optimum and then stop
The growth team's version of a loop: each variant is automatically generated, automatically measured, and once it reaches statistical significance it converges and goes live, leaving a long-term holdout, and then the next experiment begins. But Anish emphasizes that loops hit a local maximum and then plateau, and at that point you need out of distribution thinking and human intuition to land you at the foot of the next mountain. His example is telling Claude "make me a million dollars, no mistakes"—it cannot do it, because the direction has to be set by a human.

21:32 Frontier model pricing is actually irrational
Anish explains model choice using Pareto efficiency: frontier models are "irrationally priced" on the price-performance curve—one more IQ point might cost 100 times more than Opus. But for industries like drug discovery where the upside is unbounded, that one extra IQ point might be worth a trillion-dollar outcome, so paying that price is rational; for work like law and finance where the upside is bounded, you just want Pareto efficiency and use a cheap, good-enough open-weight model. The conclusion is that the two architectures will coexist, not one or the other.

31:46 People want to spend time, not save time
Anish says "loop, make me happier" is the big opportunity: people say they want to be more efficient, but actually they want to spend time—the world's biggest products are entertainment and social, not productivity tools. He distinguishes two kinds of users: AI users on X fear falling into a permanent underclass and argue endlessly about whether GLM or Kimi is stronger; Instagram users just think "this is a better Google search." He thinks this is not a model or capability problem but a product design problem: for the past 40 years we have built technology that extends the intellect, not something that extends the soul.

34:49 Consumer AI is still stuck in iPhone 2010
Anish compares the present to iPhone 2010—Airbnb, WhatsApp, and Uber had not yet appeared. Three things are holding back consumer: models are too expensive, making free products hard; the interface problem—chat only suits "the highest-agency people in the world" like Elon and Sam, while the ideal interface for ordinary consumers is TikTok, and we need to find something between chat and TikTok; and the technology has been too focused on productivity rather than human connection and entertainment. He thinks all three are now loosening: open-weight models have brought costs down dramatically, founders like Eugenia are seriously thinking about interfaces, and Brian Chesky has also started a lab focused on next-generation interfaces.

item.title: Copper grades are falling from 2% to 0.4%, while AI's power demand goes to infinity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-oddlots-铜矿品位从2-跌到0-4-ai的电力需求却要上天/
item.description: Global copper grades keep sliding, a new mine takes 35 years to permit, and an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.
item.content:encoded:
Global copper grades keep sliding, a new mine takes 35 years to permit, and an AI search uses 30x the power of a normal one — supply is shrinking, demand is exploding, and copper is becoming the new oil.

Robert Friedland draws on 40 years in mining to lay out copper's supply-demand deadlock: falling grades, 8-year equipment lead times, sulfuric acid shortages. High information density, but the real goods only come in the back half.

14:30 The next 18 years will mine all the copper of the past 10,000
Friedland offers an arithmetic that makes you squirm: humanity has mined 700 million metric tons of copper in all of history, and to recover all of it you would have to dismantle the US and Europe back to the mammoth age to get back roughly 700 million tons. But at the current pace of the global economy, just sustaining 3% GDP growth — not even counting EVs and data centers — means the next 18 years have to dig up the same amount of copper as the past 10,000 years. And people in the industry broadly think that's impossible, because the US has deindustrialized and hasn't built a single copper smelter or nuclear power plant since.

22:51 The world's largest copper mine's grade is in free fall
Friedland dissects Escondida: when this, the world's largest copper mine, was discovered a generation ago, its grade was close to 2%; today it's down to 0.8%, and within two years it will fall to 0.4%. Falling grade means crushing and grinding more rock to extract less metal, and crushing and grinding account for 4% to 5% of global energy consumption. The mine sits at 12,000 feet in the Andes, in the Atacama Desert where it hasn't rained in 30,000 years, and it takes two cubic meters of water to crush one cubic meter of rock. They built a $4 billion desalination plant and spend $1 million a day on electricity pumping water from sea level up to 12,000 feet. The upshot: just keeping this one mine producing requires another $10 to $12 billion of investment.

27:54 An AI search uses 30x the power of a normal search
Friedland gives a concrete energy comparison: one Google search consumes the electricity to light a 100-watt bulb for 12 seconds, while one AI search — he cites ChatGPT4 and Cloud — uses 30 times that, equivalent to lighting a 100-watt bulb for two or three minutes. Every five-year-old on the planet with an iPad is using AI search, and power demand ‘literally goes to infinity’. He also points out: nothing about the internet is inherently green, and this studio itself is copper-intensive and energy-intensive.

34:01 Sulfuric acid prices rose more than sixfold in eight months
About 25% of the world's copper needs sulfuric acid for leaching and extraction, and sulfuric acid comes mainly from Middle Eastern natural gas. After the Strait of Hormuz closed, sulfuric acid prices went from $150 a ton to over $1,000 a ton in eight months. Russia and China have already banned sulfuric acid exports. Friedland's company benefits, because it built Africa's largest copper smelter where sulfuric acid is a byproduct — they sell it to fellow copper miners in Congo, at ever higher prices. But he warns: without more sulfuric acid, global food prices will rise too, because sulfuric acid is also used to make fertilizer.

51:25 Buying one large motor means waiting eight years
Friedland tells a supply-chain story that is absurdly specific: building the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mine in Mongolia's Gobi, they needed large motors about 40 feet in diameter, and just the ring gear took four and a half years to arrive. Today the same equipment takes eight to ten years, ‘if ever’. And hyperscalers trying to buy natural gas turbines face lead times of six to eight years. An even more extreme example: a Congo copper mine flooded by an earthquake needed pumps to drain it, pumps moving 1,300 liters per second with a head three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. They called the US and Germany, and neither could build them, because they couldn't get samarium-cobalt magnets. Only China could build them within 30 days. At the time, the flooding was costing $15 million a day in lost revenue.

58:35 US miners cost $100 an hour; Congo engineers cost $800 a month
Friedland directly compares cost structures: Congo copper grades run 3% to 6%, the median age is 18.7, and a Congo software engineer who knows AI earns $800 to $1,000 a month. Mining copper in the US, by contrast, means the United Steelworkers demand over $100 an hour for underground work, plus environmental legislation and legal constraints, making costs far higher. He also criticizes the net present value model invented by the financial system: it was designed for oil and gas, but mines can't be shoehorned into it — an oil field decays fast if you don't invest, whereas a mine with 100 years of reserves won't deplete like an oil field. The NPV model suppresses mining company valuations, and today mining companies' total market cap is under 1% of the S&P 500, the lowest ever.

1:02:39 Tariffs could keep US copper mining alive, but they'd stoke inflation
Asked about copper tariffs, Friedland says explicitly he won't take a position, but he can argue both sides: if copper is $6 and you add a 30% tariff, that's $1.80, taking copper to $7.80, and then he can afford American miners' wages and mining in the US becomes viable. But the other side is domestic inflation, possibly higher interest rates, and with midterms coming, it's a political question. He boils it down to: do you actually want to reindustrialize America? If you can't even build nuclear plants and ships, you lose sovereignty. Last year the US built about 8 ships; China built 1,000.

1:04:42 Governments are quietly stockpiling copper, and nobody can tally supply and demand
Friedland raises an overlooked phenomenon: governments are buying copper as a proxy for money, and not reporting it. He says nobody can calculate the supply-demand balance for any metal, because ‘why would you’. Meanwhile China is buying gold and selling US Treasuries, and a great debasement trade is beginning. Hedge funds borrow yen and depend on the yen weakening so they never have to pay it back. He thinks we're at an inflection point where everything is becoming naked and globally scrutinized.

item.title: A U.S. measles death is erased from CDC data, and state reporting becomes negotiable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-twiv-美国麻疹死婴被从cdc数据里抹掉-州报告权正在被联邦接管/
item.description: The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the case: state reporting has become negotiable.
item.content:encoded:
The CDC refused to count two Pennsylvania measles deaths in the national tally, citing "insufficient information" — but the CDC itself took part in that investigation. The precedent is more dangerous than the case: state reporting has become negotiable.

A clinical-update show: the first stretch is a quick pass over outbreak data, and the two densest segments are the measles death dispute in the middle and the COVID vaccine cardiovascular benefit later.

4:06 Local dengue has shown up in Florida
Griffin says he can now see dengue cases without leaving the country: in the past week alone Florida had 32 locally acquired cases, bringing the cumulative total past 70 locally acquired dengue cases, with 14 virus-positive mosquito pools detected across 5 counties. In the same segment he notes a CDC health advisory issued that day — rabies-related consultations since July 2026 are up 17% over the same period in 2025, including mass exposure events, against a backdrop of U.S. pet owners hesitating to vaccinate animals against rabies. Put together, these two things show not an isolated event for one pathogen but that the U.S. has abandoned defenses against preventable diseases it mastered decades ago.

6:09 NIH money is being moved to the Department of Defense
Nature reported that NIH is seeking to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars of research projects from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to the Department of Defense (referred to in the piece as the Department of War) biodefense program, and two NIH employees told Nature the two sides had signed a preliminary agreement. The Defense Department response confirmed a research agreement was signed, allowing "project-by-project strategic collaboration," and said "any suggestion that this agreement was made in secret is false" — but the response never mentions the money. Griffin's follow-up is direct: biodefense itself is fine, the Defense Department has plenty of money, and it does not need to reach into the pocket of an already underfunded NIH.

9:09 HPV vaccination has not budged in four years, stuck at 77.7%
The MMWR adolescent vaccination coverage survey shows HPV vaccine coverage among 13- to 17-year-olds has not risen since 2021, now stalled for a fourth consecutive year: in 2025 only 77.7% had received at least one dose, and only 63.4% completed the series. By comparison, Tdap and meningococcal vaccines have held at about 90% since 2019, with far smaller geographic variation than HPV. The HPV vaccination gap between rural and urban areas exists at every poverty level, whereas the meningococcal rural-urban gap appears only among adolescents below the poverty line. Griffin's comment: this vaccine can prevent 100% of cervical, anogenital and head and neck cancers, so why isn't it being done.

15:15 Congo Ebola: only 15% of new cases come from known contacts
MMWR used a set of "operational indicators" to assess control of the 2026 Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo over the 21 days from July 31 to August 21: the average proportion of alerts investigated within 24 hours was 83%, against a target above 90%; an average of only 10.6 contacts were identified per confirmed case, against a target above 20; only 15% to 20% of newly confirmed cases had previously been identified as known contacts, against a target above 90%, meaning most cases are occurring outside known chains of transmission; and 59% of Ebola deaths occurred outside Ebola treatment centers, a number that should be zero. Griffin's conclusion is that the outbreak is far from controlled, with 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths to date.

17:16 The CDC removed state-reported measles deaths from the tally
On August 25 the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-related deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first in 35 years; the next day RFK Jr. suggested on X that the deaths might have been fabricated by the governor's staff. Late on Sunday, August 30, the CDC published its weekly measles update, replacing the two deaths with an asterisk and saying available information could not determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths. According to The Washington Post and CNN, the decision came from new CDC director Erica Schwarz, at RFK Jr.'s direction. Vincent points out the key fact: state and local health departments do the case investigation, apply the case definition and report to the CDC; the CDC has no independent investigative authority and historically only receives and aggregates, checking later. This time the CDC was itself embedded in the Pennsylvania investigation, so the "insufficient information" claim does not hold up.

19:18 Nobody routinely screens the dead for measles
A SIDRAP commentary dismantles the "measles wasn't the direct cause of death" line: clinically there is no admission swab, no routine testing before delivery or surgery, and no laboratory reason to go looking for measles virus in someone without symptoms; CDC guidance for clinicians says to look first at clinical features — fever, cough, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, rash — and only then mentions testing. So a positive measles result in a death investigation usually means there was already a clinical or epidemiological reason to test. The piece concedes the probability of an unrelated death coinciding with an unrelated measles infection is not zero, but small enough that a rational person should shift their judgment substantially. In the Pennsylvania case specifically: the mother also became severely ill after another child was infected with measles, delivered about a month early, and the infant was born without breathing and could not be resuscitated, with measles virus detected in lung tissue.

22:20 The structure of the death certificate is being used as a shield
Much of the dispute stems from how death certificates are filled out, something most people have never had reason to learn. Part one lists the causal chain leading to death, with the top line the immediate cause and the lines below it the conditions that produced it, ending with the underlying cause that started the sequence; part two, per the National Center for Health Statistics handbook, is "other significant conditions contributing to death." So the immediate cause line reads pneumonia, encephalitis, or in this case splenic rupture, while measles appears in part two — measles caused the splenic rupture, and the splenic rupture killed the child. Treating "the immediate cause wasn't measles" as evidence measles was irrelevant mistakes the structure of a form for a medical conclusion.

24:20 The real damage is the precedent, not these two cases
Vincent lays out the consequence clearly: if the CDC can refuse to accept a state's statutory report until it is satisfied, then the national count becomes negotiable, and every state's data is subject to federal review under undisclosed standards. Former CDC medical examiner Deb Hury told STAT that states have always reported deaths and the CDC has always counted them. Pennsylvania also pushed back on the federal account of "what information was actually provided," saying both deaths were reported to the CDC's measles response team, that the state epidemiologist conducted a thorough investigation, and that per the Pennsylvania health commissioner the CDC was in fact embedded in that investigation. Griffin adds: whichever team is in power now, someday the other team will be, and the federal government should not be touching the data.

item.title: Active management giant moves its headquarters to Nashville, saving $85 million a year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-mastersinbiz-主动管理巨头把总部搬去纳什维尔-一年省下8500万美元/
item.description: Alliance Bernstein moved from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, and forced no fund manager to relocate — the savings are real estate and people costs, the bet is on hiring people New York can't.
item.content:encoded:
Alliance Bernstein moved from New York to Nashville, saving roughly $85 million a year, and forced no fund manager to relocate — the savings are real estate and people costs, the bet is on hiring people New York can't.

A 32-year JPMorgan veteran explains the structural shifts in asset management: active to passive, ETFs replacing mutual funds, private credit entering 401ks. Medium information density; the second half is worth more than the first.

9:18 When passive squeezes active, cut costs before talking growth
The Alliance Bernstein Bernstein took over was hitting the biggest industry headwind since the financial crisis: money moving from active to passive, fees compressing across the board, institutional sales commissions falling from 20 to 25 cents a share all the way to a few cents or less than a cent. The firm itself had just been through a collapse — post-merger AUM had touched nearly $900 billion mid-quarter, and by 2012 only $380 billion remained; in 2006 roughly 70% was equity assets, and by 2012 only 30%. His predecessor, brought in from Goldman Sachs, restructured, replaced part of the teams, and equity performance began to recover, which is what got the firm back to net inflows. Bernstein says what he brought was not firefighting but a more global perspective and an emphasis on distribution.

21:39 Moving to Nashville saves $85 million a year, and no one is forced to move
The firm was debating whether it could still afford a New York headquarters, and ultimately chose Nashville from five candidate cities — the reason being ‘wanting to be a big fish in a small pond’, which Charlotte or Dallas could not deliver. The move saves roughly $85 million a year, part real estate and part people costs. The key design: no fund manager is forced to relocate, because the firm is a ‘price taker’ for that kind of talent. As a result, nearly 100 fund managers chose to move. The challenges are concrete too: Nashville is the capital of healthcare services, and locally it is hard to find international tax accountants and technology and operations people with traditional Wall Street training; but the firm received a flood of résumés from Atlanta, Chicago, New York, Boston and the West Coast.

25:44 Without cross-subsidy, sell-side research can only be a joint venture
Bernstein says a buy-side firm owning a sell-side research business is a historical accident. Almost every peer uses equity capital markets or prime brokerage to cross-subsidise its research department, and Alliance Bernstein had no such businesses to subsidise with. So they put the research business into a joint venture with Société Générale, and made clear it would eventually transition entirely to SocGen. He specifically mentions the other side's concern was culture — a large French institution facing a group of Americans and Brits — so it had to be advanced step by step, very carefully. The transition period runs five years from the JV's anniversary, and they are still midway through it.

37:08 Banks are structurally unsuited to holding long-dated fixed-rate assets
Bernstein uses his experience running leveraged finance at JPMorgan to explain the structural opportunity in private credit: banks are highly leveraged players operating on short funding, structurally unsuited to holding long-duration, especially fixed-rate, assets. JPMorgan at the time spent a great deal of time and money trying to securitise its loan book, and credit derivatives started there. Insurance companies and funds are a better home for these assets, because funds do not offer a genuine liquidity option and therefore have no run risk. He states plainly that there is no maturity transformation in credit, and apart from interest and principal there should never be any liquidity at all.

40:14 Private credit's problem is not defaults, it is insufficient disclosure
Asked how the industry gets past the first-half troubles this year, Bernstein's answer is education and transparency: tell clients how many names are on the watch list, how many have stopped accruing interest. He says there is currently no mandatory disclosure obligation, but regular updates to clients make them more comfortable, and one should ‘over-communicate in periods like this’. He also frames the problem as structural rather than systemic: defaults are simply the normal state of lending, and models typically already build in 2%, 3%, 4% default expectations; what went wrong was a handful of companies, plus fraud which has always existed; what genuinely went wrong was that structure and pricing got out of balance for a time. His conclusion is that after this episode, now is actually a better entry point.

43:14 Private credit in 401ks: fees are not the obstacle
Bernstein thinks target-date funds and 401ks may be exactly the right place for private credit: demand is highly predictable, professional managers make the decisions, and plan sponsors are themselves sophisticated investors. Alliance Bernstein worked with Brookfield and Carlisle to develop a vehicle usable alongside target-date funds, building diversified exposure to private credit, private equity and private real estate. He concedes the industry has been too optimistic about the pace of adoption, that plan sponsors are conservative, and that this will take many years, but in ten years it will most likely be part of large plans. On the fee objection, his response is: these are institutional buyers and they will drive a hard bargain; and private assets are only a small slice of a target-date portfolio, so the impact on total fees is limited.

47:18 Retirement planning should go through retirement, not stop at it
Bernstein cites Australia's superannuation funds as an example, saying they are thought leaders on how to think about retirement, and that one key practice is designing the glide path to go through retirement rather than stop at it. His reasoning: what most people need least at 65 is to hold mainly short-term fixed income and cash, because they may have another 20 to 25 years to live. More practically, many people have not saved enough to retire, and will delay retirement and look for supplementary income. He also proposes a concrete mechanism: rather than buying an annuity in one lump at retirement, design the target-date fund to leave a pool of liquidity at 75 to buy an annuity, which can significantly lower the cost of the annuity while extending income security over a longer lifespan.

51:26 AB is the last publicly traded partnership
Bernstein says AB is probably the last publicly traded partnership, a structure rare outside energy MLPs. It means issuing K-1 tax forms, and institutions have an allergic reaction to K-1s, which limits their willingness to hold the stock. He describes the stock as ‘a bond with an equity option’, essentially high-yield debt plus an equity kicker. Asked why not change the structure and give the share price a pop, his answer is direct: if they changed the structure and the stock did not pop, a lot of people would be unhappy; and most shareholders would be negatively affected on taxes, so the board has to consider it, but the honest answer is that it is not a sure thing.

item.title: The Oldest Manuscript of The Song of Roland Is Actually an English Performance Copy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-britishhist-最古老的-罗兰之歌-抄本-其实是个英国人的演出本/
item.description: The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.
item.content:encoded:
The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.

This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.

1:03 The most complete version is an English manuscript
The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France proper — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was at some point bound together with a completely unrelated book, which is why it is called Digby 23 B; A is that "other book." Who bound them together is unknown — possibly a monk who felt both were his favourite books.

3:05 Every stanza is a camera position
The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood shifts, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut in performance into four plus six: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six fall, overall close to iambic turning trochaic. Chanted over and over it becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

7:27 At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times
This kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially violent or the emotion especially strong, several consecutive laisses will tell the same action from three angles — a slow-motion sequence in poetic form. Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant, for instance, is told three times with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — "Roland dies, his soul ascends" is followed directly by "the Emperor arrives at Roncevaux."

9:29 The performer's name is left at the end of the manuscript
Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will not tell more." The line comes before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem and is not a known scribe, so scholars lean toward him being the owner of this manuscript and the performer of this repertoire.

10:31 Pocket-size dimensions give away that it was a tool of the trade
The manuscript measures only about six and a half inches by four and a half — a pocket copy you could carry on your person, not a finely bound volume for a wealthy collector. It is itself heavily worn and not refined, and contains small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to an itinerant professional performer: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator of a troupe, with someone in front of him acting out the movements. Such a person is a jongleur — the origin of the later word juggler.

12:31 The dialect pins this performer to England
The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor continental French, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests the performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant and l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French is also dropping final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

14:34 Accent drift alone can date a manuscript
Scholars' grip on this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent — and they spelled by sound.

17:40 A French epic, an English artefact
Although this is a French poem about an old French king, the manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons at the time. There is no equally complete manuscript to compare it against line by line, but there are abundant records of The Song of Roland being sung before and after this copy, and scholars can use them to judge where this performer departs from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience is constructed, and what the music sounds like.

item.title: The Army Secretary Resigns: The People Who Know How to Fight Get Cleared Out First
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-chinatalk-陆军部长辞职-最会打仗的人先被清掉/
item.description: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military has been on a treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who actually understand tech and are willing to take risk are being purged batch by batch.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the US military has been on a treadmill: budgets eaten by war, transformation forced through on cheap technology, and the officers who actually understand tech and are willing to take risk are being purged batch by batch.

The first half — the 9/11 reckoning and Army personnel insider detail — is dense with information; the second half, on AI battlefields and model distillation, is more casual chat, so you can listen to just the first half.

3:03 The war on terror ate the money for military transformation
Before 9/11 the US military was transforming as Rumsfeld demanded, under the expectation of a relatively comfortable budget environment in which new technology could be folded into the force gradually. Then GWAT arrived, all available resources were sucked into the war, and the transformation directive remained while the money was gone. The result was a run of procurement disasters: the Army's Future Combat Systems, the Navy's Ford-class carrier, the Littoral Combat Ship, DDG-1000 Zumwalt, and the CGX that was simply never built. Brian's judgment is that the technology jumped too far, the investment was nowhere near enough, and everyone was distracted supporting a war that had just started, so these programs were doomed. The troubles with today's B-21 and F-35 trace back to this period too.

5:22 Twenty-five years on a treadmill, never actually stopping
Tony points out that op-tempo never stopped after it started in 2001: 12-month and 15-month deployment rotations, with the National Guard still deploying at home and abroad today. Killing Bin Laden in 2011 could have been a high point, but nothing changed afterward — deployments continued, and through the fall of Kabul, they were still deploying. No one has fully calculated what 25 straight years in that state costs an army. Brian adds a mechanism: conventional forces used to train at home, reset, and move through a training progression, and that rhythm disappeared, replaced by "preparing for the next deployment," so there is no time to test new technology or study new ways of fighting.

7:31 MRAP thinking: use a bigger truck to stop an anti-tank missile
Brian gives an example absurd in its specificity. In Syria the threat was not IEDs but ATGMs (anti-tank guided weapons, similar to Russian TOW variants). The commander's reflex was to stuff everyone into MRAPs — making the vehicles bigger, which made them easier for ATGMs to spot, while MRAP armor cannot stop munitions designed to penetrate tanks. His conclusion: risk calculation in the war-on-terror era has gone so deep that commanders cannot reconceptualize even a small tactical adjustment. This is also the direct consequence of why so many commanders today struggle to adapt to Ukraine and the Lisko battlefield, and cannot imagine how the way of fighting will change.

9:37 Get used to zero casualties and you can't accept dying
Brian says that after 9/11 the US military became increasingly risk- and casualty-averse. The Littoral Combat Ship debate is the specimen: opponents said the ship couldn't take a hit and would be sunk the moment a war started; the original proposers answered that it was never going to be sent into a major war, and if it got sunk in a surprise attack, that was the risk you take for serving. That logic was completely unacceptable on Capitol Hill — Iraq and Afghanistan pushed casualties far below the levels of past wars, everyone got used to it, and so they cannot accept that against a peer opponent a great many people will probably die. The result is continuing to build "Death Star"-style big ships and big platforms, hoping they can protect themselves, rather than going with smaller, more distributed routes that accept a different risk structure.

10:39 Twenty-five years encircling Iran without building a network
Brian says this is the most important lesson he took from 9/11, and it came from a friend's reminder: for 25 years the US has essentially surrounded Iran, and the CIA's and part of special operations' job is to develop networks and identify people who could oppose an oppressive regime, in case a moment of change comes. But when the shooting against Iran started six months ago, it looked like very little network- and capacity-building had been done in those 25 years. The reason is a mental shift: GWAT focused on counterinsurgency and catching bad guys, not the long-term unconventional warfare of pre-positioning for a future conflict — how to support an insurgency inside a regime you might one day want to overthrow. In his words, everyone was too busy stabilizing the situation rather than destabilizing.

13:53 Driscoll resigns, and from here on it's all acting officials
Tony recaps: George was fired, Driscoll went to the White House, said "everything is terrible," and resigned that same week. The backdrop is the Army being meddled with back and forth by OSD and the Secretary of the Army's office, plus personality clashes. What he hears is that Congress will not confirm anyone else Pete nominates, so either they bring in someone both the White House and Congress can accept but Pete doesn't like, or they just keep using acting officials. He judges this is the start of the rest of this administration being "stuck with acting officials": after the midterms the House flips at least, the Senate either flips or goes 50:50, no one has the energy to push this kind of person through, and so acting officials, continued OSD meddling, and low morale will persist.

14:54 The drone battalion is disbanded, and the ability to experiment goes with it
The Army decided around the same time to dissolve the newly created drone battalion — a battalion meant to absorb Ukraine's lessons directly and then study how to embed them in infantry battalions. Tony concedes there is a good argument that "it shouldn't exist in just one battalion": concentrating lessons in one central warehouse strips every commander of the responsibility to think about organization themselves. But his worry is that the Army still needs a unit that can run experiments, run tests, and allow failure; cutting it in the name of "uniformity" loses the ability to experiment, and the force will stand still. He also names Chris Donahue as sacrificed: a commander widely recognized as understanding technology, its effects, and how to run international partnerships, done away with over the Abbey Gate bombing (not his fault) and a photo a reporter took.

21:03 Confidence is lost in layers, by rank
Tony breaks morale down by rank: junior officers are still early, but already thinking "garrison isn't what I signed up for," and that if you're not garrisoned you go get hit by missiles; field-grade officers are starting to agonize over whether they have to make political decisions just to stay in; senior field-grade officers and junior generals are basically "all in or burned out." He says the whole force is tired, and this doesn't look like the Army they joined. And in interviewees' telling, the Iran war is more of a tipping point than Donahue's departure — many O-4s and O-5s he knows supported this administration and are furious after the Donahue affair. Brian adds: people like Donahue are the true product of elite selection, and cutting them makes you doubt the claim that promotion is "by ability alone."

item.title: AI researchers speed up 10x in two years, but RSI may be easier than being a paralegal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-dwarkesh-ai-研究员两年提速-10-倍-但-rsi-可能比当律师助理更容易/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-dwarkesh-ai-研究员两年提速-10-倍-但-rsi-可能比当律师助理更容易/
item.description: RSI is a cumulative task: in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law-firm paralegal, by contrast, has to remember shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution.
item.content:encoded:
RSI is a cumulative task: in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch. A law-firm paralegal, by contrast, has to remember shifting interpersonal relationships and tacit ways of doing things — a non-stationary distribution.

The three researchers' disagreements about RSI, continual learning and RL generalisation are very concrete, and the second half's mechanistic explanation of mid-training and signal-to-noise is the most valuable part of the episode.

0:00 A model looks smart, then a month later it looks dumb again
John Schulman describes a recurring loop: a new model comes out, people are blown away and say "this is AGI", but after about a month of use it starts to look dumb again. This loop may keep repeating, and it's hard to predict how many more times. His mechanism: capability won't explode right now, because when doing research and engineering you still get stuck on bottlenecks — even if a model can write far more code than a human, that doesn't give you a 100x productivity gain. Dwarkesh opens by asking: if crazy alien superintelligence hasn't shown up by 2036, what's the most likely technical reason? Beren Millidge's default answer is a Moravec-paradox-style continuation — AI does superbly at whatever humans put into a benchmark or environment, but a stubborn sim-to-real gap always stands in the way.

18:39 Distillation is the only force against centralisation
John Schulman sees distillation as the main force countering the centralisation trend: anything learnable through RL can be easily distilled, because the number of bits is small and a little data suffices. But he stresses distillation is not trivial — when distilling with supervised learning the prompt distribution matters enormously, and you need a real, broad prompt distribution. He mentions something that has surfaced recently: some Chinese companies may be running router services that let Chinese users access otherwise-blocked US frontier models, and these services collect and sell data, which is an extremely useful dataset for distillation because it gives a perfect prompt distribution. Charlie O'Neill draws a concrete prediction from this: frontier labs may not have much of an edge left on RL environments.

44:38 RSI is a cumulative task; being a lawyer is not
Charlie O'Neill splits tasks into two kinds: cumulative and non-stationary. RSI is cumulative — in theory a Python file under a million tokens could train a recursively self-improving model from scratch, and once attention, mixture of experts or GRPO is discovered you just add it to the training stack without going back to the start. The real world is not cumulative: a law-firm paralegal has to remember the shifting relationships among all the important people in the firm and all the tacit ways of doing things, which is a non-stationary distribution. Dwarkesh's summary: "RSI just happens to be easier than being a paralegal, which is too bad." If labs conclude RSI is cumulative, more compute will tilt that way.

52:00 Continual learning is stuck on catastrophic forgetting
Charlie O'Neill says the outer loop of pouring data into mid-training at large scale and large batch does work, but at the micro level — a model doing several hundred consecutive small updates for one law firm — every method collapses: SFT on successful trajectories catastrophically forgets, and general capability degrades; on-policy distillation pushes that boundary a bit further out but eventually yields too. RL is good at injecting capability and bad at injecting knowledge. Beren Millidge thinks this is mainly a technical problem, not a capacity problem: a model of the same size pretrained from scratch on all the data is simply better, and the bottleneck is plasticity and catastrophic forgetting, with no good way to stop old data being forgotten.

59:46 Data explains 12x, architecture only 3.7x
Dwarkesh and Princeton's Jerry Han ran a grid experiment: pairing training recipes and datasets from 2019 to now in every combination, GPT-2 with the latest Ultra-FineWeb, Delphi with an old dataset like Pile, running the whole grid. The conclusion is that data gives about a 12.0x compute-efficiency gain, while architecture improvements give only about 3.7x, and at very small scale. Charlie O'Neill says the big internet chunk has already been eaten, useful things won't keep growing at the same rate, and there's probably just a pile of 0.1% loss reductions left. He notes someone at Epoch estimated 3x per year since 2019, over 2000x cumulative, and the missing 100x probably comes from post-training.

1:03:00 RL needs a curriculum; pretraining doesn't
Beren Millidge says this comes back to the RL signal problem: RL is currently bad at exploration, and if the model can't get it in 128 rollouts there's basically no learning signal, so RL needs curricula while pretraining needs none at all. Charlie O'Neill adds: the pretraining signal is already in Common Crawl, the problem is just filtering out noise, which can be automated; but once you get to mid-training and post-training the signal simply isn't in the raw data, and no amount of filtering will extract it — there isn't a Millennium Prize proof hiding in Common Crawl waiting to be sifted out. You have to get the bits elsewhere: have people write out reasoning traces, construct environments, or use human data from deployment.

1:18:03 Most of RL's success comes from mid-training
Beren Millidge says what's underrated is mid-training: pretraining on synthetic reasoning data and environments, warm-starting the model to almost the end of the road to the final RL checkpoint, with RL only fine-tuning the policy on top. So it doesn't need to learn these behaviours from scratch, and a few bits per episode are enough. He also stresses that the signal-to-noise of those bits is far higher than ordinary pretraining — in SFT you have to match another model's reasoning trace token by token, which injects too many bits about "how it thinks" and drowns the signal; RL's objective ignores all the other bits and keeps only "did it get the answer right".

1:28:32 One year or three, the difference is long-tail chores
Asked when you could hire a drop-in remote white-collar worker, Charlie O'Neill says if it has to operate a browser, probably a few years; if it can be given Slack and programmatic access, probably a year. Beren Millidge says full generality might be three years, but organisations will actively reshape themselves to be more AI-friendly, so 80-90% is reachable before then. The substance of the disagreement is the long tail: some chores humans can do will take models a long time. Charlie gives the example that a model won't "yell at people" to push work forward — it's too nice. John Schulman points out that human remote workers already vary enormously in quality, and on Upwork it's often hard to get someone doing a software project to take feedback seriously; in some cases the pre-AI version is worse than today's AI.

item.title: The Clippers Used Fake Endorsements to Skirt the Cap, and the NBA's Law Firm Found More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-moneystuff-快船用假代言绕工资帽-nba-请律所查出了更多/
item.description: Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers — it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers and ending up with Kawhi Leonard.
item.content:encoded:
Wachtell's independent investigation did not clear the Clippers — it made the scandal bigger: beyond Aspiration, there is a string of fake endorsements funded by the Clippers and ending up with Kawhi Leonard.

The first half is dense with sports-scandal detail; the second half — Apollo's "jerk premium" and the Cede & Co stock custody mechanism — is the part that is actually worth money.

2:04 The Clippers used fake endorsements to get around the salary cap
The Clippers first paid millions of dollars to a company called Aspiration Partners, nominally for vague environmental services; Aspiration then paid that money to Kawhi Leonard in the form of endorsement fees, while Leonard did almost no endorsing. When Pablo Torre first reported it, the claim was still disputed, and the Clippers consistently denied it, but the investigation the NBA commissioned from Wachtell Lipton basically confirmed it — and found more similar arrangements.

4:09 Even the scoreboard company was pulled in to move the money
What the Wachtell report found was not just the Aspiration payment. The Clippers also paid "consulting fees" to companies that provided no consulting services at all, including the company that made the scoreboard for their arena. The method: the Clippers would pay a consulting fee, then call and ask for a higher purchase price on the scoreboard, with the clear expectation that the other side would pass the money on to Kawhi Leonard. The money went in a circle, and the ultimate purpose was still to give the star player a raise.

7:09 An independent law firm investigation is not there to clear you
Max had assumed an outside law firm's independent investigation was meant to produce a clean bill of health after a scandal, but the Wachtell report made things look worse. Matt offers a more cynical explanation: the classic use of a law firm investigation, under the shadow of a DOJ or regulatory probe, is to hand over some "bad apple" as a scapegoat so the company gets credit for cooperating. But this time there was no DOJ pressure to shut down the NBA, the NBA seems to have given Wachtell a lot of room, and Wachtell clearly had a great time digging.

10:14 Once the DAT premium vanished, the arbitrage ran in reverse
Empery Digital was originally an electric motorcycle company, and in July 2025 it transformed into a digital asset treasury company (DAT), stockpiling about $500 million of bitcoin, with its stock at one point trading at a premium to its holdings. The logic: put $1 of bitcoin into a DAT and it becomes $2 of stock. But the premium quickly disappeared and DATs began trading at a discount, so the arbitrage flipped — use $0.90 of stock to buy $1 of bitcoin, buy the DAT, break it up, sell the bitcoin. DAT activism was born.

17:20 Is a shareholder who shorts bitcoin disloyal
One of the core disputes in the Empery case: activists buy discounted DAT stock while shorting an equal amount of bitcoin, making themselves delta neutral and earning only the discount convergence. The company argues this must be disclosed, because the other shareholders are all theoretically long bitcoin, while these people are bitcoin neutral, their interests are not aligned, and they should not be eligible to run for the board. Matt thinks the argument is "wrong, but only accidentally wrong": if a DAT is a vehicle for believers to hold bitcoin (like Strategy), it makes sense; but most DAT shareholders are the same hedge funds, all of whom came for the premium and are unhappy about the discount, so their interests are actually aligned.

23:26 Cede & Co holds most American stocks
Matt mentioned in his column a fact most people do not know: most shares of most American companies are registered in the name of Cede & Co, the nominee of the DTC. A 1998 report said Cede & Co held 83% of all American stocks; the DTC now custodies about $74 trillion of stock. When you hold shares through Robinhood, what actually happens is that Robinhood has a record on the DTC's ledger, and Cede & Co is on the company's shareholder register. The system grew out of the efficiency revolution of the 1960s and 1970s, when paper stock certificates were centralised in one place and only name changes were recorded.

27:31 Robinhood's tokenisation is not an on-chain shareholder register
Tokenised stock can mean many things, and one ideal version is this: every company maintains a public blockchain shareholder register, no longer needing intermediaries like the DTC or Robinhood, and the company can build a direct relationship with its shareholders. But that is not what Robinhood did — it bought AMC stock itself, then issued derivative securities on-chain representing that stock and sold them to overseas investors, effectively "making its own copy of AMC stock." AMC's Adam Aaron was unhappy, and Vlad Tenev asked "what's the problem?"

31:35 Apollo pays 100 basis points for its "aggressive" reputation
A paper measures the reputation of private equity sponsors in three ways: having ChatGPT and Claude rank the most aggressive PE firms; looking at who has done liability management exercises (quasi-forced debt swaps); and putting Apollo in one bucket by itself and the other 24 firms in another. The conclusion: the most aggressive sponsors' portfolio companies borrow at noticeably higher yields, Apollo's loans are about 100 basis points more expensive than other sponsors', and the average yield in the sample is 717 basis points. Matt calls it the "jerk premium" or the "aggression premium" — creditors expect to be squeezed, so they charge upfront.

item.title: The foldable isn't the future of the phone — it's a two-in-one for a subset of people
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cn1b5ef7-折叠屏不是手机的未来-是给一部分人的二合一/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-cn1b5ef7-折叠屏不是手机的未来-是给一部分人的二合一/
item.description: Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the bar phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus that costs you grip and performance.
item.content:encoded:
Foldables have sold into the tens of millions, but the inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time. They won't replace the bar phone; for people who want a phone-plus-iPad two-in-one they're a plus, and for everyone else they're a minus that costs you grip and performance.

A solo episode with a product manager's eye that covers the real experience of using a foldable, the business logic behind Apple entering, and the judgment that phone form factors will diverge rather than converge. Medium information density; the back half is worth more than the front half.

12:17 The foldable's home turf is China and nowhere else
In 2025 China's full-year foldable shipments broke ten million units, with Huawei taking 70% — a crushing share. But globally, China is the largest single market, accounting for more than 40% of shipments. Which is to say this category isn't evenly distributed the way other phone form factors are; its core user is the Chinese boss holding a Huawei foldable in first class and at social occasions. On the broad view, foldables are only 2.5% of global phone shipments, and only 15% of Huawei's own phone shipments.

20:23 The inner screen gets opened less than 30% of the time
Liu Fei used a foldable as his daily driver for over half a month, and in the end didn't want to keep them. The biggest problem wasn't the crease, the camera, or the battery — it was the scenario. The inner screen doesn't get opened much: it's unstable in one hand and prone to shaking, and it's more for two-handed use, but in that scenario he'd already be carrying a 10-inch iPad. A Vivo vice president said at a launch that foldables keep getting better, but the core way you use them is no different from seven years ago, and many users open the inner screen less than 30% of the time. His analogy: it's like carrying a phone case with a built-in power bank — your phone's weight goes up permanently, but most of the time you don't need to charge, so you'd be better off carrying a separate external power bank.

23:25 Once it gets wider, scrolling feeds actually gets worse
To accommodate the outer screen, wide-expanding foldables like the Huawei Pure X Max and the Apple iPhone Door got wider, and scrolling feeds becomes very bad. Xiaohongshu is fine, because it's been adapted; but scrolling Meituan to filter restaurants, or Taobao to filter shops, the information that fits on each screen suddenly shrinks. This isn't purely an adaptation problem, it's an aspect-ratio problem: list feeds run vertically, so widening is meaningless — the height shrinks, and you see less at a glance. He recalls that ordering takeout on Meituan, he could only see three restaurants at a time.

29:33 Area grows 76%, but widescreen video actually gets smaller
A large foldable unfolded is almost square, which is a disaster for watching video and looking at photos. By screen area, opening the inner screen adds 76%, nearly double; but if you're watching a widescreen film, the foldable's inner screen effective area actually drops by 10%, because it can't fit it. Watching 16:9 content does get bigger, but only by 20%, which is fairly limited. The wide-expanding form factor has more sensible dimensions and higher effective area, but a 16:10 wide-expanding foldable playing 16:9 video still leaves 10% black bars top and bottom. The point isn't that area naturally grows — it's what you actually want to do with the inner screen.

37:38 Who the two-in-one is a plus for
Liu Fei says the most important decision logic for whether to buy a foldable is: does it add to or subtract from your old experience. He himself has a full set of devices — a Windows PC for gaming, a MacBook for work, an iPad for shows — so a foldable is pointless for him. But for many young people, the phone is their only computing device, and a lot of work happens on the phone, offline, so a bigger screen makes the experience much better. Salespeople who travel constantly and need to present a deck to a client in a café get a much better result from the inner screen than the outer one. Put another way: what you're buying isn't a bar phone that turns into a tablet, it's a foldable iPad mini.

45:47 Without AirPods there'd be no Chinese podcasting
Liu Fei says the Apple Watch and AirPods developed during Cook's tenure are both world-changing products, and AirPods especially so: without AirPods ushering in the era of Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones, you could say there'd be no podcast market, and especially no Chinese podcast market. Chinese podcasting took off in sync with Bluetooth noise-cancelling headphones — because only with noise cancelling can you hear clearly what someone is saying while commuting, working out, or doing chores. Before that, those scenarios were usually for listening to music, or to content with very low information density.

57:04 Apple's kill shot is migrating the iPad ecosystem
On hardware, the iPhone Door doesn't have such an overwhelming advantage; it uses materials from a mature supply chain, weighs 254 grams, and perceptibly isn't that different from Android flagship foldables. The core advantage is that Apple has the iPad: since the iPad launched in 2010, the 4:3 ratio has accumulated an enormous content ecosystem, and a lot of software was already optimized well enough for that ratio before foldable phones even existed, so it can be ported straight to the iPhone Door. For Android that's a crushing level of ecosystem migration. On top of that, Apple did a lot of optimization on one-handed interaction, putting frequently used buttons on the dominant-hand side — that's a system-level design, and it's relatively easy for developers to follow and adapt to.

1:08:09 How you define success decides whether it succeeds
Whether the iPhone Door succeeds depends on how you define success. If you define it as replacing the bar phone, it's nearly impossible; if you define it as becoming a product line that keeps selling, it's very possible. First-generation shipments of a few million units shouldn't be a problem, and it might even reach ten million — JD reservations have already passed 500,000. Liu Fei says phone form factors won't converge, they'll diverge: the bar phone is the only form factor the whole world would vote for, but other form factors will keep existing and keep differentiating, at every price point and in every shape. Foldables won't replace bar phones, even if performance, experience and price were exactly the same, because a substantial number of people simply have no need to open an inner screen.

item.title: Americans Suddenly Fell in Love With Japan — Not Because It's Cheap, Because It's Normal
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-searchengine-美国人突然爱上日本-不是因为便宜-是因为它太正常了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-11-searchengine-美国人突然爱上日本-不是因为便宜-是因为它太正常了/
item.description: The real driver of Japan's tourism explosion isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space — clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.
item.content:encoded:
The real driver of Japan's tourism explosion isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space — clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.

This episode uses expert interviews plus a listener survey to break "why is everyone going to Japan" into six verifiable reasons; the back half, on Japanese craft culture versus American dysfunction, is especially worth hearing.

1:05 One visitor's spreadsheet: 119 people, and the problem is out of control
The questioner, Lisa, is a Japanese person living in Tokyo. She made a visitor calendar running from November 2022 to April 2026, with green squares marking days someone visited. She counted 119 people, 96 of them her own guests, averaging one person every five days — 20% of all her days. She says she spends all her free time helping visiting friends plan their trips. The data visualization is itself evidence that the problem has spun out of control, and it's the starting point for the question this episode sets out to answer.

8:34 Japan is poor in resources, rich in story
Roland Kelts argues the first reason for American interest in Japan isn't economic, it's narrative. He says Japan has almost no natural resources, no oil, very little land, only small rice paddies — but a story culture that is astonishing. The world's first novel is Japanese, The Tale of Genji, a thousand years old. Through manga, anime and the internet, the whole world discovered this narrative capacity. This didn't start in the 1990s; Roland says there were two earlier waves: Japanism in late 19th-century Europe, and the Beats' and hippies' fascination with Zen and Buddhist concepts in the 50s and 60s.

15:05 America used to be afraid of Japan
David Marks points out that for seventy years after World War II, mainstream American feeling toward Japan was fear, not affection. Before 1945 Japan was an enemy nation; afterward it was seen as a developing country rebuilding itself. In the 70s and 80s it became anxiety about Japanese economic power, and Michael Crichton's Rising Sun cast Japan as the villain. After the Cold War ended there was even a CIA position paper discussing whether Japan should be the next enemy. When Japan's economic bubble burst in the 90s, America felt something like relief. When David moved to Japan in 2003, a friend visiting Japan was the event of the year, because basically nobody came.

24:29 The government deliberately made Japan cheap
The third wave was a government plan. In 2003 Junichiro Koizumi launched the Visit Japan campaign, aiming to raise the target from 5 million tourists a year to 10 million, with ads full of Western stereotypes — geisha, cherry blossoms, temples. But what actually worked was Shinzo Abe deliberately weakening the yen in the 2010s. The intent was to help exports; the result was making hotels and restaurants cheap for foreigners. Roland says you can eat a very good soba lunch in Tokyo for under $10, while in New York $10 won't even buy you an apple and a banana. In 2013 Abe relaxed visas for Thailand and Malaysia, then China and Indonesia; Asian tourists surged first, and European and American tourists followed.

29:37 Japan's functionality is the biggest draw
